blocks.title: R1: route between VLANs
blocks.text: The physical router interface has no IP address in this fixture. VLAN 999 has no gateway address or end hosts.
items: enable
configure terminal
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
no ip address
no shutdown
interface GigabitEthernet0/0.10
encapsulation dot1Q 10
interface GigabitEthernet0/0.20
encapsulation dot1Q 20
interface GigabitEthernet0/0.999
encapsulation dot1Q 999 native
end

blocks.title: Read the modes and parameters
blocks.text:
enable moves from User EXEC (>) to Privileged EXEC (#). configure terminal enters global configuration. vlan creates/selects a VLAN; name is entered in VLAN configuration mode. interface selects interface configuration. switchport mode access fixes the data port role; switchport access vlan selects its VLAN.

switchport mode trunk fixes trunking. native vlan sets the untagged-native association. allowed vlan replaces the permitted list; use add when deliberately extending an existing list. no shutdown removes administrative shutdown but cannot repair a missing cable.

On R1, encapsulation dot1Q binds a subinterface to a VLAN; native marks the untagged-native association. ip address creates the gateway address. end returns to Privileged EXEC. copy running-config startup-config saves the working configuration after verification.

blocks.title: Data and voice on one access port | objective and fixture
blocks.text:
SW1 Fa0/10 connects to a compatible Cisco phone; PC-A is behind the phone. Data VLAN 10 uses 192.168.10.0/24; voice VLAN 30 uses 192.168.30.0/24. VLAN gateways/DHCP/voice services and uplinks carrying both VLANs are preconfigured. Use a Catalyst IOS platform supporting this voice-VLAN syntax and CDP; this is separate from the two-department pilot fixture.

Instructional configuration for an isolated lab, not a live connection. Unsupported commands must not be entered into the offline trainer as if it were full IOS.

blocks.title: Data and voice on one access port | configuration
blocks.text: Copy only into the stated device/context after capturing its baseline.
items: enable
configure terminal
vlan 10
name DATA
vlan 30
name VOICE
interface FastEthernet0/10
switchport mode access
switchport access vlan 10
switchport voice vlan 30
cdp enable
no shutdown
end
show interfaces FastEthernet0/10 switchport

blocks.title: Data and voice on one access port | command purpose and modes
blocks.text: enable selects Privileged EXEC; configure terminal selects global configuration. vlan/name create and label each local VLAN. interface selects Fa0/10. mode access establishes the data-port role; access vlan 10 classifies ordinary untagged PC traffic. voice vlan 30 advertises the voice association to a compatible phone, which tags its voice traffic. cdp enable requires global CDP to be enabled as well. no shutdown enables the port; end returns to EXEC. This is a multi-VLAN access-port feature, not a general interswitch trunk. QoS trust requirements vary by platform and are not silently assumed.

blocks.title: Use evidence from both ends
blocks.text:
Run show vlan brief, show interfaces trunk, show interfaces FastEthernet0/1 switchport, and show mac address-table on each switch. On R1 use show ip interface brief and show ip route connected. Check actual port membership, operational trunk state, allowed/active/forwarding VLAN lists, and connected gateway networks before pinging.

A VLAN shown as active does not prove the trunk carries it. A trunk shown as trunking does not prove VLAN 20 is allowed. MAC entries appear only after traffic has been learned.

blocks.title: Interpret before testing
blocks.text:
If VLAN 20 is active but missing from the allowed list, will PC-C reach its gateway through this trunk?

Explain your reasoning before opening the answer.
items: No. VLAN existence does not override trunk filtering. Restore VLAN 20 on the relevant trunks, verify the forwarding list, and then test the gateway.

blocks.title: show vlan brief
blocks.text: Compare healthy and abnormal evidence in a declared fixture.

inspector.fixture: SW1 Fa0/1 is Finance VLAN 10; Fa0/2 is Engineering VLAN 20; Gi0/1 is a trunk. VLANs 10/20 exist.
inspector.healthy:
VLAN Name                 Status    Ports
10   FINANCE              active    Fa0/1
20   ENGINEERING          active    Fa0/2
inspector.abnormal:
VLAN Name                 Status    Ports
10   FINANCE              active    Fa0/1, Fa0/2
20   ENGINEERING          active

fields.label: Ports
fields.healthy: Fa0/2 belongs to VLAN 20.
fields.abnormal: Fa0/2 is in VLAN 10; the host IP is not automatically changed.

fields.label: Status

inspector.question: Engineering cannot reach its gateway. What mismatch is visible?
inspector.answer: Fa0/2 is assigned to VLAN 10 instead of 20. Verify the physical host port, correct switchport access vlan 20, then check gateway reachability.

blocks.title: Data and voice on one access port | verification and expected result
blocks.text: Inspect administrative/operational mode, Access Mode VLAN 10, and Voice VLAN 30 in show interfaces Fa0/10 switchport. Confirm the phone learned VLAN 30 and the PC remains in VLAN 10. Check DHCP leases and both gateways. A phone that powers up has not necessarily obtained voice connectivity.

blocks.title: Failure 1: PC-C cannot reach its gateway
blocks.text:
Symptom: PC-B reaches 192.168.10.1, but PC-C cannot reach 192.168.20.1. Possible causes include the wrong access VLAN, VLAN 20 missing from a trunk, wrong host mask/gateway, or a router subinterface problem.

Start with PC-C's IP settings, then SW2 Fa0/2 switchport membership. Check both switches' trunk lists and R1's subinterface. Do not infer an ACL problem before proving the local forwarding path.

If show interfaces trunk reveals only 10,999 allowed on SW2 Gi0/1, the evidence identifies a missing VLAN 20, not a failed physical link.

blocks.title: Correct the demonstrated allowed-list failure
blocks.text: On SW2, add VLAN 20 without replacing other permitted VLANs. Check the peer and SW1-to-R1 trunk as well, then ping PC-C's gateway and PC-A. A successful ping tests ICMP reachability, not every application service.
items: configure terminal
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
switchport trunk allowed vlan add 20
end
show interfaces trunk

blocks.title: Correct an access-port assignment instead
blocks.text: Use only when evidence shows the wrong access VLAN. Moving a port to VLAN 20 does not automatically change the PC's IP address.
items: configure terminal
interface FastEthernet0/2
switchport access vlan 20
end
show interfaces FastEthernet0/2 switchport

blocks.title: Safe undo in the training fixture
blocks.text:
Capture the original configuration before the exercise. Restore the original access VLAN and trunk lists explicitly; removing an allowed-list restriction can permit more VLANs, not fewer. Shut the training router parent interface before removing subinterfaces with no interface GigabitEthernet0/0.10, .20, and .999 in global configuration.

Do not delete VLANs still used by other ports. Removing a VLAN does not safely migrate its hosts. Undo is a planned restoration, not indiscriminately adding no before every command.

blocks.title: Mistakes to avoid
blocks.text: Use these checks when the evidence does not fit your first hypothesis.
items: Expecting hosts in different VLANs to communicate without routing.
Looking for trunk ports in 'show vlan brief' output.
Leaving unused ports in VLAN 1 (security best practice is to move them to an unused VLAN and shut them down).

blocks.title: Data and voice on one access port | correction and safe restoration
blocks.text: If the PC works but the phone does not, check voice-VLAN discovery, VLAN 30 uplink eligibility, DHCP/voice services, and phone compatibility. Restore the captured voice/access/CDP settings; no switchport voice vlan removes the exercise voice association. Do not delete VLAN 30 while other phones use it.

blocks.title: Choose the forwarding boundary
blocks.text:
PC-A broadcasts ARP for PC-B. Which receives it: PC-B, PC-C, both, or neither?

Explain your reasoning before opening the answer.
items: PC-B receives it because it shares VLAN 10 and the trunk carries VLAN 10. PC-C is in VLAN 20. Both is wrong because trunks preserve VLAN separation. Neither is wrong under the stated forwarding assumptions. PC-C alone reverses the VLAN memberships.

blocks.title: Reason about the header
blocks.text:
After R1 forwards PC-A's packet to PC-C, which addresses change: Ethernet MACs, original IP endpoints, both, or neither?

Explain your reasoning before opening the answer.
items: Ethernet MAC addresses change because R1 constructs a new frame for VLAN 20. Original IP endpoints do not change without NAT. Both confuses routing with translation. Neither ignores the new link-layer frame. IP-only is the reverse of ordinary routing; TTL and checksum are separate IP fields that do change.

blocks.title: Explain the failure
blocks.text:
A learner says: the trunk is up, so every VLAN must work. What evidence would you request?

Explain your reasoning before opening the answer.
items: Request allowed, active, and forwarding VLAN lists on both ends, access-port membership, and host/gateway settings. Trunking proves the operational link role, not every VLAN's eligibility or end-to-end reachability.

lessons.title: Trunking: 802.1Q and the Native VLAN
lessons.simple: A trunk is a link that carries many VLANs between switches (or to a router). Each frame gets a small tag saying which VLAN it belongs to, so the receiving switch can keep VLANs separate.

deep.heading: Tagging
deep.text: 802.1Q inserts a 4-byte tag between the source MAC and EtherType fields. The tag contains a 12-bit VLAN ID, which is why VLAN IDs go up to 4094 (0 and 4095 are reserved).

deep.heading: The native VLAN
deep.text: Frames in the native VLAN cross the trunk untagged. The default native VLAN is 1. Both ends must agree; a native VLAN mismatch is reported by CDP and can leak traffic between VLANs. Best practice is to set the native VLAN to an unused VLAN on both ends.

deep.heading: Configuration and DTP
deep.text: interface Gi0/1 / switchport trunk encapsulation dot1q (needed only on switches that also support ISL) / switchport mode trunk / switchport trunk native vlan 99 / switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,30. Add later with 'switchport trunk allowed vlan add 40' (omitting 'add' replaces the list). DTP negotiates trunking: 'dynamic desirable' actively tries; 'dynamic auto' waits. auto + auto = access; desirable + auto/desirable/trunk = trunk. Disable DTP with 'switchport nonegotiate' on trunks and by setting access ports to 'switchport mode access'. Verify with 'show interfaces trunk' (mode, encapsulation, native VLAN, allowed and active VLANs).

lessons.why: Every multi-switch network depends on trunks. Allowed-VLAN lists and native VLAN mismatches are favorite exam troubleshooting scenarios.

examples.title: Accidental replacement
examples.text: An engineer types 'switchport trunk allowed vlan 40' intending to add VLAN 40. VLANs 10-30 stop working because the list was replaced.

examples.title: DTP outcome
examples.text: SW1 port dynamic auto, SW2 port dynamic auto → the link becomes an access link, not a trunk.

mistakes: Forgetting the 'add' keyword when changing an allowed VLAN list.
Mismatched native VLANs on two ends of a trunk.
Assuming auto + auto forms a trunk.

terms.definition: IEEE standard for VLAN tagging on trunk links.
VLAN whose frames are sent untagged on an 802.1Q trunk (default VLAN 1).
Dynamic Trunking Protocol, Cisco proprietary trunk negotiation.
Legacy Cisco trunking protocol (obsolete).

memorize: 802.1Q tag = 4 bytes; TPID 0x8100; 12-bit VLAN ID.
Native VLAN is untagged; default native VLAN 1; must match on both ends.
DTP: auto+auto = access; desirable+auto = trunk.
show interfaces trunk.
examNotes: Read 'show interfaces trunk' carefully: 'allowed', 'allowed and active in management domain', and 'forwarding state and not pruned' are different lists.
lessons.summary: Trunks carry multiple VLANs using 802.1Q tags; the native VLAN is untagged and must match. Control allowed VLANs carefully and disable DTP where it is not needed.

quiz.question: How large is the 802.1Q tag?
quiz.explanation: The 802.1Q tag is 4 bytes; the VLAN ID field inside it is 12 bits.

quiz.question: Two switch ports are both 'dynamic auto'. What is the result?
quiz.explanation: Neither side initiates, so the link stays access.

quiz.question: Which command adds VLAN 50 to an existing trunk allowed list?
quiz.explanation: Use the 'add' keyword to append without replacing.

blocks.title: Start with the problem
blocks.text: Finance users on two switches need one shared VLAN without a separate interswitch cable for every department. A trunk multiplexes several VLANs on one link while keeping their forwarding identities separate.

blocks.title: Build the mental model
blocks.text: For non-native VLANs in this fixture, the switch inserts an 802.1Q tag after the source MAC field. The receiver reads the VLAN ID and forwards within that VLAN. With untagged native behavior, a native-VLAN mismatch can classify untagged traffic differently at each end. Native tagging and some control traffic are platform-dependent exceptions; inspect the actual configuration.

blocks.text: Open this explanation when you are ready for the full mechanism.
items: A trunk is a link that carries many VLANs between switches (or to a router). Each frame gets a small tag saying which VLAN it belongs to, so the receiving switch can keep VLANs separate.

blocks.title: Why this matters in practice
blocks.text: Open this explanation when you are ready for the full mechanism.
items: Every multi-switch network depends on trunks. Allowed-VLAN lists and native VLAN mismatches are favorite exam troubleshooting scenarios.

blocks.title: Tagging
blocks.text: Open this explanation when you are ready for the full mechanism.
items: 802.1Q inserts a 4-byte tag between the source MAC and EtherType fields. The tag contains a 12-bit VLAN ID, which is why VLAN IDs go up to 4094 (0 and 4095 are reserved).

blocks.title: The native VLAN
blocks.text: Open this explanation when you are ready for the full mechanism.
items: Frames in the native VLAN cross the trunk untagged. The default native VLAN is 1. Both ends must agree; a native VLAN mismatch is reported by CDP and can leak traffic between VLANs. Best practice is to set the native VLAN to an unused VLAN on both ends.

blocks.title: Configuration and DTP
blocks.text: Open this explanation when you are ready for the full mechanism.
items: interface Gi0/1 / switchport trunk encapsulation dot1q (needed only on switches that also support ISL) / switchport mode trunk / switchport trunk native vlan 99 / switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,30. Add later with 'switchport trunk allowed vlan add 40' (omitting 'add' replaces the list). DTP negotiates trunking: 'dynamic desirable' actively tries; 'dynamic auto' waits. auto + auto = access; desirable + auto/desirable/trunk = trunk. Disable DTP with 'switchport nonegotiate' on trunks and by setting access ports to 'switchport mode access'. Verify with 'show interfaces trunk' (mode, encapsulation, native VLAN, allowed and active VLANs).

blocks.title: Separate the similar ideas
blocks.text: An access port classifies ordinary untagged endpoint traffic into its access VLAN. A trunk carries multiple VLANs. Native VLAN controls the conventional untagged association; the allowed list controls which VLANs may cross. These settings are independent, and neither creates the VLAN on the peer.

blocks.title: Use the technical vocabulary
blocks.text: Read the term and explain its role before checking the definition.
rows: IEEE standard for VLAN tagging on trunk links.
VLAN whose frames are sent untagged on an 802.1Q trunk (default VLAN 1).
Dynamic Trunking Protocol, Cisco proprietary trunk negotiation.

blocks.title: Read the relationships
blocks.text: In the tag diagram, locate destination MAC, source MAC, tag, original type, and payload. The tag adds four bytes; it does not replace the IP destination. Label a VLAN 10 frame tagged across the trunk and untagged toward an ordinary access host.

blocks.title: Existing conceptual illustration
blocks.text: This bundled illustration supports the concept; exact scenario-specific diagrams remain subject to visual review.

blocks.title: Follow the behavior
blocks.text:
1. SW1 receives an untagged frame on a VLAN 10 access port.
2. It associates the frame with VLAN 10.
3. On the trunk, VLAN 10 is tagged because native is 999.
4. SW2 reads tag 10 and checks VLAN/forwarding eligibility.
5. It removes the tag when sending to an ordinary VLAN 10 access host. A trunk is not inter-VLAN routing.

blocks.title: Accidental replacement
blocks.text: Open this explanation when you are ready for the full mechanism.
items: An engineer types 'switchport trunk allowed vlan 40' intending to add VLAN 40. VLANs 10-30 stop working because the list was replaced.

blocks.title: DTP outcome
blocks.text: Open this explanation when you are ready for the full mechanism.
items: SW1 port dynamic auto, SW2 port dynamic auto → the link becomes an access link, not a trunk.

blocks.title: Fixture, command context, and restoration
blocks.text: Apply on both isolated Catalyst-style switches, Gi0/1 to Gi0/1, with fixed 802.1Q support. vlan creates local VLANs; interface selects the link; mode trunk fixes the role; native vlan sets untagged association; allowed vlan replaces the list. Expect trunking with native 999 and eligible VLANs 10/20/999 after convergence. Restore captured native/list/mode settings for undo; no allowed-list restriction can broaden access.

rationales: A trunk preserves Layer 2 separation and does not create routing.

blocks.title: Explain it in your own words
blocks.text: Trunks carry multiple VLANs using 802.1Q tags; the native VLAN is untagged and must match. Control allowed VLANs carefully and disable DTP where it is not needed.

lessons.title: Inter-VLAN Routing
lessons.simple: Devices in different VLANs are in different subnets, so a Layer 3 device must route between them. You can do this with a router using subinterfaces (router-on-a-stick) or with a Layer 3 switch using SVIs.

deep.heading: Why routing is needed
deep.text: VLAN 10 (192.168.10.0/24) and VLAN 20 (192.168.20.0/24) are separate networks. Hosts send off-subnet traffic to their default gateway, which must have an interface in each VLAN.

deep.heading: Router-on-a-stick (ROAS)
deep.text: One physical router interface connects to a switch trunk and is split into subinterfaces: interface Gi0/0.10 / encapsulation dot1Q 10 / ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0. Repeat for each VLAN. The physical interface must be 'no shutdown'. For the native VLAN, use 'encapsulation dot1Q 99 native' (or put the IP on the physical interface).

deep.heading: Layer 3 switch SVIs and routed ports
deep.text: Enable routing with 'ip routing'. Create SVIs: interface vlan 10 / ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0 / no shutdown. An SVI is up/up only if the VLAN exists and at least one access or trunk port forwarding that VLAN is up. Routed ports ('no switchport' plus an IP address) turn a switch port into a router-like interface for links to routers or other Layer 3 switches. SVIs scale far better than ROAS because routing happens in switch hardware.

lessons.why: Every enterprise network routes between VLANs. Gateway placement determines performance and where ACLs are applied.

examples.title: Small branch ROAS
examples.text: One router Gi0/0 trunked to the switch with subinterfaces .10, .20, .30 serving three VLANs.

examples.title: Campus distribution
examples.text: A Layer 3 switch has SVIs for 12 VLANs and routed uplinks to the core using OSPF.

mistakes: Forgetting 'ip routing' on a Layer 3 switch.

blocks.title: Start with the problem
blocks.text: Finance can reach Finance across switches, but not Engineering in another VLAN. That is expected Layer 2 separation. Inter-VLAN routing adds a deliberate Layer 3 path rather than weakening the VLAN boundary.

blocks.title: Build the mental model
blocks.text: A host uses its mask to select the local gateway for a remote subnet. The gateway receives a frame addressed to itself, removes Layer 2 encapsulation, looks up the destination IP, and builds a new frame for the outgoing VLAN. Original IP endpoints normally remain unchanged; TTL decreases. ACLs can control the newly possible routed communication.

lessons.title: Layer 2 Discovery: CDP and LLDP
lessons.simple: CDP and LLDP let directly connected devices tell each other who they are: hostname, model, interface, IP address, and capabilities. They are invaluable for documenting and troubleshooting networks.

deep.heading: What they share
deep.text: Device ID (hostname), local and remote interface, platform/model, capabilities (router, switch, phone), software version, and management IP address. They only see directly connected neighbors.

deep.heading: CDP
deep.text: Cisco Discovery Protocol is Cisco proprietary and enabled by default on Cisco devices. It sends advertisements every 60 seconds with a 180-second holdtime. Commands: 'cdp run' / 'no cdp run' (global), 'cdp enable' / 'no cdp enable' (interface), 'show cdp neighbors', 'show cdp neighbors detail' (includes IP addresses and IOS version), 'show cdp entry NAME'.

deep.heading: LLDP
deep.text: Link Layer Discovery Protocol (IEEE 802.1AB) is vendor-neutral and typically disabled by default on Cisco IOS. Default timer 30 seconds, holdtime 120 seconds. Commands: 'lldp run' (global), 'lldp transmit' and 'lldp receive' (interface, separately controllable), 'show lldp neighbors', 'show lldp neighbors detail'. Disable discovery protocols on untrusted, internet-facing, or user ports, because they reveal information attackers can use.

lessons.why: When documentation is wrong or missing, CDP/LLDP tell you exactly what is plugged into each port.

lessons.title: EtherChannel and LACP
lessons.simple: EtherChannel bundles several physical links into one logical link. You get more bandwidth and redundancy, and Spanning Tree treats the bundle as a single link so it does not block the extras.

deep.heading: The problem it solves
deep.text: Two parallel links between switches would form a loop, so STP would block one. EtherChannel makes both active as one logical port-channel.

deep.heading: Negotiation protocols
deep.text: LACP (IEEE 802.3ad / 802.1AX) modes: active (initiates) and passive (responds). PAgP (Cisco) modes: desirable and auto. 'on' forces a channel with no negotiation. Working combinations: active+active, active+passive, desirable+desirable, desirable+auto, on+on. passive+passive and auto+auto do not form. Never mix 'on' with a negotiating mode.

deep.heading: Configuration and verification
deep.text: interface range Gi0/1 - 2 / channel-group 1 mode active. This creates interface Port-channel1; configure trunk/VLAN settings on the port-channel. Members must match in speed, duplex, switchport mode, access VLAN or trunk allowed/native VLANs. A Layer 3 EtherChannel uses 'no switchport' on the members and the Port-channel and an IP address on the Port-channel. blocks.title: Start with the problem
blocks.text: Two switches need more aggregate capacity and a backup path. Simply adding parallel Layer 2 cables can create a loop or cause STP to block one. EtherChannel groups compatible links into one logical port-channel.

blocks.title: Build the mental model
blocks.text: Member links must have compatible operational and configuration attributes. The switch distributes flows using a hash over selected header fields; one ordinary flow generally stays on one member rather than gaining the sum of all link speeds. STP treats a Layer 2 bundle as one logical link. Losing one member can reduce capacity without taking the whole channel down.

lessons.title: Spanning Tree Protocol and Rapid PVST+
lessons.simple: Redundant switch links are good for reliability but create Layer 2 loops, which cause broadcast storms and MAC table instability. Spanning Tree Protocol (STP) prevents loops by logically blocking some ports while keeping them ready as backups.

deep.heading: Why loops are dangerous
deep.text: Ethernet frames have no TTL. A broadcast entering a loop circulates forever, multiplying until links and CPUs are saturated (a broadcast storm). STP builds one loop-free tree.

deep.heading: How STP elects roles
deep.text: 1) Elect the root bridge: lowest Bridge ID (priority, default 32768 + VLAN ID as system ID extension, then lowest MAC). 2) Every non-root switch picks one root port: lowest root path cost (default short costs: 10 Mbps = 100, 100 Mbps = 19, 1 Gbps = 4, 10 Gbps = 2), then lowest neighbor bridge ID, then lowest neighbor port ID. 3) Each segment gets one designated port (on the switch with the lowest cost to the root). All root bridge ports are designated. 4) Remaining ports are blocked (alternate).

deep.heading: Rapid PVST+ details
deep.text: Rapid PVST+ runs one RSTP (802.1w) instance per VLAN. Port roles: root, designated, alternate (backup path to root), backup (redundant port on the same segment). Port states: discarding, learning, forwarding (legacy 802.1D had blocking, listening, learning, forwarding, disabled with 15 s forward delay and 20 s max age). Commands: 'spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst'; 'spanning-tree vlan 10 root primary' (sets priority 24576 or lower) / 'root secondary' (28672); or 'spanning-tree vlan 10 priority 4096' (multiples of 4096). Edge features: 'spanning-tree portfast' (access ports go straight to forwarding); 'spanning-tree bpduguard enable' (err-disables a PortFast port that receives a BPDU); 'spanning-tree guard root' (prevents a port from becoming root port; puts it into root-inconsistent state); 'spanning-tree guard loop' (stops a port that stops receiving BPDUs from becoming designated); 'spanning-tree bpdufilter enable' (stops sending/receiving BPDUs, use with care). Verify: 'show spanning-tree vlan 10'.

lessons.why: A single misplaced cable without STP can take down an entire campus within seconds. Controlling root bridge placement keeps traffic on optimal paths.

examples.title: Root election

examples.title: Root port tie
examples.text: SW3 has two equal-cost paths via SW2; it chooses the path through the neighbor with the lower bridge ID.

mistakes: Using a priority not a multiple of 4096.
Thinking the root bridge has a root port (it has none; all its ports are designated).
Enabling PortFast on switch-to-switch links without BPDU Guard.
Forgetting that the lowest (not highest) bridge ID wins.

PortFast + BPDU Guard on access ports; Root Guard where the root must never appear.

Know what each guard feature does and the resulting port state (err-disabled for BPDU Guard; root-inconsistent for Root Guard; loop-inconsistent for Loop Guard).
lessons.summary: STP prevents Layer 2 loops by electing a root bridge, root ports, and designated ports, and blocking the rest. Rapid PVST+ converges quickly per VLAN, and PortFast, BPDU Guard, Root Guard, and Loop Guard protect the topology.

blocks.title: Build the mental model
blocks.text: BPDUs carry topology/election information. Priority and the extended system ID participate in bridge identity; MAC address breaks an otherwise equal comparison. Path cost and subsequent tie-breakers determine port roles. Rapid states are discarding, learning, and forwarding. PortFast accelerates edge-port transition; it does not disable STP. BPDU guard protects intended edge ports; root guard, loop guard, and BPDU filtering have distinct purposes and must not be treated as interchangeable.

lessons.title: Cisco Wireless Architectures and AP Modes
lessons.simple: Access points can work alone (autonomous), be centrally controlled by a WLC (lightweight), or be managed from the cloud. How APs and controllers connect to switches depends on which mode they use.

deep.heading: Three architectures
deep.text: Autonomous APs are configured one by one and handle everything themselves. Lightweight APs split the work with a WLC (split-MAC): the AP handles real-time functions like beacons and encryption; the WLC handles authentication, RF management, roaming, and policy. Cloud-based (e.g., Meraki) APs are managed through a cloud dashboard.

deep.heading: CAPWAP and deployment models
deep.text: Lightweight APs build CAPWAP tunnels to the WLC: control on UDP 5246 (always DTLS-encrypted) and data on UDP 5247 (encryption optional). WLC deployments include centralized/unified (dedicated appliance), cloud-hosted (e.g., Catalyst 9800-CL), embedded (WLC in a switch), and Mobility Express/EWC (controller running on an AP).

deep.heading: AP modes and physical connections
deep.text: Modes: Local (default; all client traffic tunneled to WLC), FlexConnect (can switch client traffic locally and survive WAN outage), Monitor (no clients; sensors for rogue/IDS/location), Sniffer (captures traffic to an analyzer), Rogue detector, SE-Connect (spectrum analysis), Bridge/Mesh. Physical: a Local-mode AP connects to an access port (its management VLAN), since client traffic is inside CAPWAP. A FlexConnect AP locally switching multiple VLANs connects to a trunk port. A WLC connects to a trunk because it serves many VLANs (dynamic interfaces). blocks.title: Start with the problem
blocks.text: A branch AP can be online while its controller connection is unavailable. Whether users can still pass traffic depends on architecture and switching mode, not simply whether the AP has a radio.

blocks.title: Build the mental model
blocks.text: CAPWAP separates control and data relationships between AP and controller. The AP management network must reach the controller, but client VLANs depend on where traffic is switched. A centrally switched AP uplink may not need every client VLAN locally; a locally switched multi-VLAN AP may require a trunk. Controller and switch LAG support depends on platform and design.

WLC distribution ports are often bundled with LAG, which on AireOS WLCs requires a static EtherChannel ('channel-group X mode on') because the WLC does not negotiate LACP or PAgP.

lessons.title: Interpreting WLAN Configuration in the WLC GUI
lessons.simple: Creating a wireless network on a Cisco WLC is done in a web GUI. You define the WLAN (SSID), map it to a VLAN interface, choose security settings, and pick a QoS profile.

deep.heading: Creating a WLAN
deep.text: In the AireOS GUI: WLANs > Create New > Go. Enter a profile name, the SSID, and a WLAN ID. On the General tab, set Status to Enabled and choose the Interface/Interface Group (which maps clients to a VLAN).

deep.heading: Security tab
deep.text: Layer 2 Security: WPA+WPA2 (or WPA2/WPA3 on newer releases); WPA2 Policy with AES encryption. Authentication Key Management: PSK (personal) with a passphrase of 8-63 ASCII characters, or 802.1X (enterprise) with a RADIUS server defined under the AAA Servers tab.

deep.heading: QoS and Advanced tabs
deep.text: QoS profiles: Platinum (voice), Gold (video), Silver (best effort, default), Bronze (background). Advanced tab includes options such as session timeout, client exclusion, Aironet IE, DHCP address assignment required, and FlexConnect local switching. On Catalyst 9800 controllers the workflow uses WLAN profiles, policy profiles, and tags, but the concepts are the same.

lessons.why: The exam can show WLC GUI screenshots and ask what a setting does or why clients cannot connect.

lessons.title: Device Management Access
lessons.simple: Network devices can be managed locally through a console cable or remotely over the network. Remote access must be secure: use SSH instead of Telnet and HTTPS instead of HTTP, and authenticate administrators centrally with AAA when possible.

deep.heading: Access methods
deep.text: Console: direct serial (RJ-45 rollover or USB), default 9600 baud, works even with no IP configuration. Telnet (TCP 23): remote CLI, everything in clear text. SSH (TCP 22): encrypted remote CLI. HTTP (TCP 80) / HTTPS (TCP 443): web GUI. Cloud-managed: devices are controlled from a cloud dashboard.

deep.heading: Configuring SSH
deep.text: hostname R1 / ip domain-name example.com / crypto key generate rsa modulus 2048 / ip ssh version 2 / username admin secret StrongPass1 / line vty 0 4 (0 15 on switches) / login local / transport input ssh. On a switch, you also need a management IP (e.g., an SVI) and 'ip default-gateway' if the switch is not routing. Verify with 'show ip ssh' and 'show ssh'.

deep.heading: File transfer and centralized authentication
deep.text: TFTP (UDP 69) is simple, has no authentication or encryption, and is used for copying IOS images and configurations: 'copy running-config tftp:'. FTP (TCP 21 control, TCP 20 active data) supports username/password authentication but is clear text; SFTP/SCP add encryption. TACACS+ and RADIUS let devices authenticate administrators against a central server (covered in AAA). Disable unused services such as 'no ip http server' when only HTTPS is required ('ip http secure-server').

lessons.why: Remote management is how almost all network devices are operated. Insecure protocols expose credentials to anyone capturing traffic.

examples.title: Secure baseline
examples.text: VTY lines accept only SSH with local usernames; HTTP server disabled; HTTPS enabled for the GUI.

examples.title: Image upgrade
examples.text: Engineer runs 'copy tftp: flash:' to download a new IOS image from a TFTP server.

Using RSA modulus below 768 bits, which prevents SSHv2.
Forgetting 'login local' so VTY lines ignore the local user database.
Assuming FTP is encrypted.

lessons.title: Routing Fundamentals and the Routing Table
lessons.simple: A router decides where to send each packet by looking up the destination IP address in its routing table. The table lists known networks, how the router learned them, and which next hop or interface to use.

deep.heading: How a router forwards
deep.text: For each packet, the router removes the Layer 2 frame, reads the destination IP, finds the best matching route, decrements the TTL, builds a new frame for the outgoing interface (with the next hop's MAC), and sends it. If no route matches and there is no default route, the packet is dropped.

deep.heading: Reading 'show ip route'
deep.text: Codes: C = connected, L = local (the router's own /32 interface address), S = static, O = OSPF, S* = static default route (candidate default). Example: 'O 10.2.2.0/24 [110/2] via 10.0.0.2, 00:05:12, GigabitEthernet0/1'. Components: route source, destination prefix and mask, [administrative distance/metric], next hop, route age, and outgoing interface. 'Gateway of last resort' shows the default route.

deep.heading: Choosing the best route
deep.text: 1) Longest prefix match always wins: for 10.1.1.5, a /24 route beats a /16 beats a /0. 2) If the same prefix is learned from different sources, the lowest administrative distance (AD) wins: connected 0, static 1, eBGP 20, EIGRP 90, OSPF 110, IS-IS 115, RIP 120, iBGP 200, unusable 255. 3) If the same prefix comes from the same protocol, the lowest metric wins (OSPF metric = cost). Equal-cost paths can be load-shared (ECMP). Remember: AD and metric are only compared between routes to the exact same prefix.

lessons.why: Reading a routing table correctly is the single most important IP Connectivity skill and a core exam topic (25% domain).

examples.title: AD decision
examples.text: 10.5.5.0/24 is learned by OSPF (AD 110) and configured as static (AD 1). The static route is installed.

mistakes: Comparing AD between routes with different prefix lengths (longest match is evaluated first).
Thinking the router chooses the lowest metric across different protocols.
Forgetting about the local (L) /32 routes added for each interface IP.

blocks.title: Start with the problem
blocks.text: A router has several routes that seem to match one packet. The key is to separate building the routing table from forwarding a packet through that table. The most trusted route source is not always the most specific forwarding match.

blocks.title: Build the mental model
blocks.text: A routing entry identifies prefix, source code, next hop or directly connected interface, and often administrative distance/metric. A default route /0 matches anything but loses to a more specific matching installed route. Connected networks require operational interfaces. The forwarding implementation may use a FIB derived from the routing table rather than perform a text-table search per packet.

blocks.title: Revisit the core explanation
blocks.text: Open this explanation when you are ready for the full mechanism.
items: A router decides where to send each packet by looking up the destination IP address in its routing table. The table lists known networks, how the router learned them, and which next hop or interface to use.

blocks.title: Why this matters in practice
blocks.text: Open this explanation when you are ready for the full mechanism.
items: Reading a routing table correctly is the single most important IP Connectivity skill and a core exam topic (25% domain).

blocks.title: How a router forwards
blocks.text: Open this explanation when you are ready for the full mechanism.
items: For each packet, the router removes the Layer 2 frame, reads the destination IP, finds the best matching route, decrements the TTL, builds a new frame for the outgoing interface (with the next hop's MAC), and sends it. If no route matches and there is no default route, the packet is dropped.

blocks.text: Longest prefix match chooses the most specific installed matching prefix. Administrative distance helps choose between route sources for the same prefix. A routing protocol metric compares paths within that protocol. These are different decisions, not three interchangeable numbers.

lessons.title: Static Routing for IPv4 and IPv6
lessons.simple: A static route is a route you type in manually. It is simple, predictable, and uses no bandwidth for routing updates, but it does not adapt automatically when the network changes.

deep.heading: Basic syntax
deep.text: 'ip route <destination network> <mask> <next-hop IP | exit interface>'. Example: ip route 192.168.20.0 255.255.255.0 10.0.0.2. The route appears in the table as 'S' with AD 1.

deep.heading: Types of static routes
deep.text: Network route: a specific subnet. Default route: 'ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 203.0.113.1' matches everything (S*). Host route: a /32 such as 'ip route 10.9.9.9 255.255.255.255 10.0.0.2'. Floating static route: a backup route with an AD set higher than the primary, e.g., 'ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 198.51.100.1 130' stays out of the table while an OSPF-learned default (AD 110) exists.

deep.heading: IPv6 static routes and next-hop choices
deep.text: Enable 'ipv6 unicast-routing'. 'ipv6 route 2001:DB8:2::/64 2001:DB8:12::2', default 'ipv6 route ::/0 GigabitEthernet0/1 FE80::2'. When the next hop is a link-local address, you must specify the exit interface as well. Using only an exit interface on an Ethernet (multi-access) link is discouraged for IPv4 because the router relies on proxy ARP; prefer next-hop or fully specified routes. A static route is only installed if its next hop is reachable (or exit interface is up). Verify with 'show ip route static' and 'show ipv6 route static'.

lessons.why: Static routes are used at network edges (default route to an ISP), in stub branches, and as backups to dynamic routing.

examples.title: Branch default route
examples.text: ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 10.255.0.1 sends all non-local traffic to HQ.

examples.title: Floating backup
examples.text: Primary default learned via OSPF (AD 110); backup 'ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 172.16.99.1 200' takes over only if OSPF's route disappears.

mistakes: Setting a floating route AD lower than the primary, so it becomes the primary.
Using a link-local next hop without an exit interface in IPv6.
Forgetting the return route on the remote router (traffic goes out but replies cannot come back).

0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0; matches any destination.

blocks.title: Start with the problem
blocks.text: A small branch has one path to head office. Rather than run a dynamic protocol, you can explicitly tell its router which next hop reaches the remote prefix. A static route is that instruction; it still needs a reachable next hop and a return path.

blocks.title: Build the mental model
blocks.text: Next-hop routes depend on recursive resolution to an outgoing path. A link-local IPv6 next hop requires the outgoing interface to disambiguate scope. A floating route can remain unused while a failed upstream path still leaves the preferred route installed; tracking is a separate mechanism. Never describe administrative distance as a reachability probe.

blocks.title: IPv6 network, host, default, and floating routes | command purpose and modes
blocks.text: All ipv6 route lines are global configuration. /64 selects a network, /128 selects one host, and ::/0 is the default. The final 200 is administrative distance for the backup /64. The /128 wins forwarding for that host while installed, even if the /64 changes. To test /64 failover, use another host such as ::30 or remove the exercise host route. A link-local next hop instead requires an outgoing interface, for example ipv6 route 2001:DB8:20::/64 GigabitEthernet0/0 FE80::2 when that peer address is verified.

blocks.title: What evidence should show
blocks.text: Use show ip route static, show ip route 192.168.20.20, and show ip interface brief. For IPv6 use show ipv6 route static. Confirm the route is installed, not just present in running configuration. Test from a source that exercises the intended return path.

inspector.answer: No. Verify the intended static route and next-hop resolution, install/correct it, and confirm the return route. DNS does not create a forwarding path.

blocks.title: IPv6 network, host, default, and floating routes | verification and expected result
blocks.text: Expect the preferred /64, host /128, and default to be installed if next hops resolve. The distance-200 /64 is normally not the selected route while the preferred /64 exists. Inspect show ipv6 route for a chosen destination. A remote service outage does not necessarily remove the preferred static; tracking is a separate feature.

blocks.title: Diagnose, correct, and retest
blocks.text: If the static is configured but absent from the table, check next-hop resolution and interface state. If outbound packets arrive but replies fail, inspect the remote return route and policy. Correct the specific route, verify installation, then retest from the original client subnet.

blocks.title: Mistakes to avoid
blocks.text: Use these checks when the evidence does not fit your first hypothesis.
items: Setting a floating route AD lower than the primary, so it becomes the primary.
Using a link-local next hop without an exit interface in IPv6.
Forgetting the return route on the remote router (traffic goes out but replies cannot come back).

blocks.title: IPv6 network, host, default, and floating routes | correction and safe restoration
blocks.text: If the route is absent, verify next-hop reachability and interface state. If return traffic fails, inspect R2 routes and policy. Undo each exact route with its no form, including the distance on the floating route. Do not remove the shared transit addressing as part of route cleanup.

blocks.title: Apply the idea
blocks.text: A floating static has distance 200 while OSPF installs the same prefix at distance 110. Which is preferred?
items: Both because distance is a load-sharing weight
Neither because static routes cannot have a distance
OSPF while its route remains installed
The floating static because 200 is larger
rationales: Distance is not a proportional load-sharing weight.
IOS supports a configured administrative distance on static routes.
Lower administrative distance is preferred for competing sources to the same prefix.
A larger distance makes this static less preferred.

blocks.title: Explain it in your own words
blocks.text: Static routes provide manual, predictable paths: network, host, default, and floating routes for IPv4 and IPv6, with floating routes acting as backups via higher AD.

lessons.title: OSPFv2 Single Area
lessons.simple: OSPF is a link-state routing protocol. Routers form neighbor relationships, share information about their links, build an identical map of the network, and use Dijkstra's SPF algorithm to calculate the shortest path to every network.

deep.heading: Link-state in plain terms
deep.text: Each OSPF router describes its links in Link-State Advertisements (LSAs). All routers in an area store these LSAs in the link-state database (LSDB). Every router independently runs SPF on the same LSDB to build its routing table. Cost is the metric: lower is better.

deep.heading: Neighbors and adjacencies
deep.text: Routers send Hellos to 224.0.0.5 every 10 seconds (dead interval 40 s on broadcast and point-to-point networks). Neighbor states: Down → Init (Hello received) → 2-Way (saw own RID in neighbor's Hello) → ExStart (master/slave chosen) → Exchange (DBDs exchanged) → Loading (LSRs/LSUs) → Full. To become neighbors, routers must match: area ID, subnet/mask, Hello and dead timers, authentication, and stub flag; they need unique router IDs, and MTU must match to reach Full.

deep.heading: Network types, DR/BDR, router ID, cost, and configuration
deep.text: On broadcast networks (Ethernet default), a DR and BDR are elected to reduce flooding: highest interface priority (default 1; 0 = never), then highest router ID. The election is non-preemptive. DROTHERs reach Full only with the DR and BDR and stay 2-Way with each other; updates to DR/BDR use 224.0.0.6. On point-to-point networks ('ip ospf network point-to-point'), no DR/BDR is elected. Router ID: manually set ('router-id 1.1.1.1'), else highest loopback IP, else highest active physical interface IP. Cost = reference bandwidth (default 100 Mbps) / interface bandwidth; change with 'auto-cost reference-bandwidth 10000' (in Mbps) or 'ip ospf cost'. Configure: router ospf 1 / network 10.0.12.0 0.0.0.3 area 0 (wildcard mask) or interface-level 'ip ospf 1 area 0'; 'passive-interface Gi0/2' (stop Hellos on user LANs while still advertising them); 'default-information originate' to advertise a default route. Verify: show ip ospf neighbor, show ip ospf interface [brief], show ip protocols, show ip route ospf.

lessons.why: OSPF is the most widely used enterprise interior routing protocol and the only dynamic routing protocol you configure on the CCNA.

examples.title: Two routers on a /30
examples.text: R1 and R2 on 10.0.12.0/30, area 0, network type point-to-point. Both show FULL/ - with no DR/BDR.

examples.title: Adjacency failure
examples.text: R1 Hello 10/Dead 40, R2 Hello 5/Dead 20 → they never become neighbors. 'show ip ospf interface' reveals the timer mismatch.

examples.title: DR election
examples.text: Three routers on a LAN; R3 has priority 255 → R3 is DR (if it is up when the election runs).

mistakes: Using a subnet mask instead of a wildcard mask in the 'network' command.
Expecting OSPF process IDs to match between neighbors (they are locally significant).
Expecting DROTHERs to be FULL with each other.
Forgetting that DR election does not preempt; raising priority later has no effect until a re-election.

Shortest Path First (Dijkstra) algorithm.
32-bit dotted-decimal ID unique to each OSPF router.
Designated Router / Backup DR on multi-access networks.
Advertised network on which no Hellos are sent.
Backbone area; single-area OSPF uses only area 0 in most designs.

memorize: Hello 10 s, Dead 40 s (broadcast/P2P). AD 110. Multicast 224.0.0.5 (all) and 224.0.0.6 (DR/BDR).
States: Down, Init, 2-Way, ExStart, Exchange, Loading, Full.
Neighbor must-match: area, subnet, timers, authentication, stub flag; unique RID; MTU for Full.
RID order: manual → highest loopback → highest active interface.
Cost = 100 Mbps / bandwidth (default reference).
examNotes: 'show ip ospf neighbor' output reading is heavily tested: FULL/DR, FULL/BDR, 2WAY/DROTHER, FULL/ - (point-to-point).
Process ID is local; area must match.
lessons.summary: OSPFv2 forms adjacencies using Hellos, synchronizes LSDBs, and computes shortest paths with SPF using cost. Know neighbor requirements, states, DR/BDR election, router ID selection, and configuration/verification commands.

quiz.question: Which value must match for two OSPF routers to become neighbors?
quiz.explanation: Area ID must match; process IDs are locally significant and RIDs must be unique.

quiz.question: Two DROTHERs on the same LAN will settle in which state?
quiz.explanation: DROTHERs remain 2-Way with each other.

quiz.question: With default reference bandwidth, what is the cost of a FastEthernet (100 Mbps) interface?
quiz.explanation: 100/100 = 1. (Gigabit is also 1, which is why the reference is often raised.)

quiz.question: Which command stops OSPF Hellos on a LAN interface but still advertises its subnet?
quiz.explanation: passive-interface.

blocks.title: When static routes become a maintenance problem
blocks.text:
Two branches are connected by routers. Each router knows its directly connected networks, but not the LAN behind the other router. Static routes could teach those destinations. As the network grows or links fail, manually maintaining every route becomes difficult.

OSPF, Open Shortest Path First, lets routers describe their links and build a shared topology view within an area. Each router then calculates its own best paths. Think of sharing road maps rather than accepting a neighbor's directions blindly. The analogy stops at the calculation: OSPF uses configured link costs, not live road congestion.

blocks.title: Map, calculation, and forwarding table
blocks.text:
A link-state advertisement (LSA) describes topology information. The link-state database (LSDB) holds the advertisements. Shortest Path First (SPF) calculates paths from the local router's perspective. Eligible routes are offered to the routing table.

These are different objects. Two routers in the same area aim to synchronize their area LSDBs, but their shortest-path trees and next hops differ because each starts from itself. An OSPF neighbor relationship is not proof that every desired route has been installed.

blocks.title: Scope and simulation boundary
blocks.text: Required CCNA v1.1 objective 3.4: single-area OSPFv2, neighbor adjacencies, point-to-point, broadcast DR/BDR selection, and router ID. Packet-exchange detail supports understanding. This lesson uses authored simulated IOS output. The offline CLI trainer does not implement OSPF.

blocks.title: Static routes versus OSPF
blocks.text:
A static route is an administrator's explicit forwarding instruction. OSPF learns topology and recalculates after changes. Static routes remain useful for simple paths and defaults; OSPF is not automatically better for every network.

For competing routes to the same prefix, Cisco administrative distance helps select the source; OSPF cost chooses among OSPF paths. Forwarding then uses longest prefix match among installed routes. Do not compare administrative distance across different prefix lengths to make a forwarding decision.

blocks.title: Broadcast Ethernet versus point-to-point
blocks.text:
On broadcast Ethernet, routers elect a designated router (DR) and backup (BDR) to limit full adjacency relationships. Two DROTHER routers normally remain 2-Way with each other. Each becomes fully adjacent with the DR and BDR.

On an OSPF point-to-point network, there is no DR/BDR election; the two routers can become fully adjacent directly. The configuration below explicitly selects point-to-point even though the physical link is Ethernet. Network type is protocol behavior, not just the cable type.

blocks.title: Point-to-point command fixture
blocks.text:
R1 Gi0/0 = 10.0.12.1/30 connects directly to R2 Gi0/0 = 10.0.12.2/30. Both use area 0 and point-to-point network type.

R1 Loopback0 = 192.168.1.1/32; router ID = 1.1.1.1. R2 Loopback0 = 192.168.2.1/32; router ID = 2.2.2.2. Both advertise the loopback passively.

The fixture sets the transit interface cost to 10 and loopback cost to 1 on both routers. R1's cost to R2's loopback is therefore 11. No competing static route or other routing protocol is configured.

blocks.title: Identity comes before discovery
blocks.text:
The router ID is a 32-bit OSPF identifier displayed like an IPv4 address; it need not be a reachable interface address. Configure it explicitly for predictable labs. On common IOS behavior, absent an explicit ID, selection prefers the highest loopback IPv4 address, then the highest active non-loopback IPv4 address when the process selects its ID.

Changing a configured router ID may require restarting the OSPF process to take effect. That disrupts adjacencies; do not clear a production process casually.

blocks.title: Watch the neighbor relationship develop
blocks.text:
1. Down: no recent valid Hello from the neighbor.
2. Attempt: applicable to manually configured NBMA neighbors, not a mandatory step on this point-to-point link.
3. Init: R1 receives R2's Hello but does not yet see its own router ID in R2's neighbor list.
4. 2-Way: R1 sees its own ID in the received Hello; bidirectional discovery is established. Whether to form a full adjacency depends on network type and role.
5. ExStart: neighbors negotiate database-description exchange roles and initial sequencing.
6. Exchange: Database Description (DBD) packets summarize LSA headers.
7. Loading: Link State Requests (LSRs) request needed advertisements; Link State Updates (LSUs) carry LSAs, and Link State Acknowledgments (LSAcks) acknowledge advertisements.
8. Full: the adjacency's database synchronization is complete. Loading may be brief or unnecessary if nothing needs requesting. This is a conceptual progression, not a claim that every adjacency visibly pauses in every state.

blocks.title: What the packets actually carry
blocks.text:
OSPFv2 runs directly over IPv4 protocol 89, not TCP or UDP. Hello packets discover and maintain neighbors. DBD packets summarize databases; they are not the complete LSDB. An LSU can carry multiple LSAs; an LSA is not itself one of the five OSPF packet types.

224.0.0.5 is AllSPFRouters; 224.0.0.6 is AllDRouters. On broadcast networks, DROTHERs use AllDRouters for applicable flooding toward the DR/BDR, while the DR floods to AllSPFRouters. Some exchanges are unicast; not every OSPF packet uses multicast. Point-to-point behavior does not introduce a DR just because multicast is used.

blocks.title: DR/BDR and cost details
blocks.text:
On broadcast networks, priority determines election eligibility and preference; priority 0 is ineligible. Router ID breaks ties. Elections are not simply preempted when a higher-priority router joins. The DR is an adjacency/flooding role, not the default gateway or necessarily the best transit path.

Cisco automatic cost is based on reference bandwidth divided by interface bandwidth, with a minimum cost of 1 and integer treatment. Interface bandwidth is an administrative value, not measured throughput.
items: Classic IOS commonly uses a 100-Mbps reference bandwidth, so faster links can all receive cost 1. Verify the platform and configuration. auto-cost reference-bandwidth uses Mbps and should be planned consistently across the OSPF domain. An explicit ip ospf cost overrides automatic interface cost. This fixture uses explicit costs to make the expected route metric deterministic.

blocks.title: Hello compatibility: what must match
blocks.text:
Two routers become OSPF neighbors only if their Hellos agree on the parameters OSPF checks. On a shared segment they must agree on the area ID, the Hello and dead intervals, the authentication settings, and the area type flags (for example, stub). On broadcast and NBMA networks the subnet and mask must also match. Router IDs must be unique.

Cisco IOS defaults on broadcast and point-to-point networks are a 10-second Hello and a 40-second dead interval; changing one side alone prevents the neighbor relationship. Interface MTU is not a Hello field: it is checked in Database Description packets, which is why an MTU mismatch typically leaves neighbors stuck in ExStart or Exchange instead of preventing discovery.

OSPF process IDs are locally significant and do not need to match. Network type is not a Hello compatibility field, but mismatched types (one side broadcast, the other point-to-point) can produce a neighbor that never reaches a working Full adjacency or routes that do not install as expected, so keep both ends consistent as this fixture does.

packet.assumptions: Authored OSPFv2 point-to-point area 0 progression, not a live routing process. Both interfaces use matching Hello/Dead intervals 10/40, matching authentication policy and compatible MTU. Loopback advertisements and cost 10+1=11 match the pilot. Fields are selected explanatory values, not a complete byte-level packet capture. Packet types may repeat; this is a successful representative sequence, not a promise of exact packet counts.

devices.name: R1
devices.details: 10.0.12.1/30; router ID 1.1.1.1; area 0; outgoing cost 10; point-to-point.

devices.name: R2

steps.title: Down: no valid neighbor information
steps.action: No valid Hello has established the neighbor relationship.
steps.why: Down is a neighbor state, not necessarily a physically down interface.
steps.next: Receive a valid Hello.

steps.title: Init: receive a Hello
steps.action: R1 receives a Hello from R2 that does not yet list R1.
steps.why: R1 knows R2, but bidirectional recognition is not established.
steps.next: A subsequent valid Hello lists R1.

steps.title: 2-Way: bidirectional recognition
steps.action: R2 lists R1 router ID 1.1.1.1 in a valid Hello.
steps.why: On this point-to-point link the routers proceed toward adjacency. Broadcast DROTHER pairs can remain 2-Way normally.
steps.next: Begin database synchronization.

headers.DR/BDR election: Not used on this point-to-point link

steps.title: ExStart: negotiate database exchange
steps.action: Neighbors establish database-description sequencing and roles.
steps.why: Persistent ExStart requires evidence such as MTU and router-ID checks, not an automatic single-cause diagnosis.
steps.next: Exchange database summaries.

headers.Purpose: Negotiate exchange sequencing; not application data

steps.title: Exchange: describe the database
steps.action: Neighbors exchange Database Description packets containing LSA header summaries.
steps.why: A summary identifies available LSAs; it is not necessarily the complete LSA content.
steps.next: Request missing/newer information if needed.

steps.title: Loading: request and receive missing LSAs
steps.action: A neighbor requests missing/newer LSAs and receives Link State Updates.
steps.why: Loading may be brief or unnecessary when nothing is missing.
steps.next: Acknowledge reliable flooding and complete synchronization.

steps.title: Acknowledge LSA delivery
steps.action: Use the protocol acknowledgment behavior for reliable LSA flooding.
steps.why: Type 5 is a Link State Acknowledgment packet; it is not a TCP ACK.
steps.next: Reach Full when required database synchronization is complete.

steps.title: Full: adjacency synchronized
steps.action: The intended adjacency is Full; SPF derives routes from the synchronized topology.
steps.why: Full is not proof that every destination/application works. Routing, ACLs, and return paths still matter.
steps.next: Inspect the remote loopback route.

blocks.title: Objective and IOS context
blocks.text: Configure two isolated IOS/IOS XE routers supporting interface-based OSPFv2. Interface names may differ. Start with no existing OSPF process 1 or competing route for the loopbacks. The commands intentionally set router IDs before enabling interfaces. They are instructional configurations, not commands supported by the offline trainer.

blocks.title: R1: identity, interfaces, and area
blocks.text: The transit link exchanges Hellos; the loopback is advertised without forming neighbors.
items: enable
configure terminal
router ospf 1
router-id 1.1.1.1
passive-interface default
no passive-interface GigabitEthernet0/0
exit
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
ip ospf network point-to-point
ip ospf cost 10
ip ospf 1 area 0
no shutdown
interface Loopback0
ip ospf cost 1
ip ospf 1 area 0
end

blocks.title: R2: matching area and network type
blocks.text: Area 0 and compatible link parameters are shared. Router IDs must be unique; process numbers are locally significant and need not match.
items: enable
configure terminal
router ospf 1
router-id 2.2.2.2
passive-interface default
no passive-interface GigabitEthernet0/0
exit
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
ip ospf network point-to-point
ip ospf cost 10
ip ospf 1 area 0
no shutdown
interface Loopback0
ip ospf cost 1
ip ospf 1 area 0
end

blocks.title: Explain the configuration modes
blocks.text:
enable enters Privileged EXEC; configure terminal enters global configuration. router ospf 1 creates/selects local process 1 and enters router configuration. router-id assigns its identity. passive-interface default suppresses OSPF neighbor exchanges on interfaces by default; no passive-interface permits them on the transit interface.

exit returns from router to global configuration. interface enters interface configuration. ip address assigns the link address and mask. ip ospf network point-to-point selects the OSPF network type. ip ospf cost sets the outgoing cost. ip ospf 1 area 0 enables process 1 on that interface in area 0. end returns to Privileged EXEC.

An alternative network/wildcard command under router configuration selects local interfaces for OSPF; it does not mean advertise any arbitrary remote network. This fixture uses interface-based activation to make the relationship explicit.

blocks.title: Verify identity, adjacency, database, and route separately
blocks.text:
On both routers, run show ip ospf, show ip ospf interface GigabitEthernet0/0, show ip ospf neighbor, show ip ospf database, and show ip route ospf.

Check router ID, area, network type, cost, timers, passive status, and neighbor address. Then inspect the remote loopback route. Full adjacency is necessary for this fixture, but it is not proof that the remote loopback was enabled in OSPF.

blocks.title: R1# show ip ospf neighbor: simulated excerpt
blocks.text: Authored simulated IOS-style excerpt, not a live connection. Neighbor ID is R2's OSPF identity; Address is R2's transit IP. FULL indicates synchronized adjacency. The dash means no DR/BDR role on this point-to-point network. Timer formatting and displayed priority can vary by platform.
items: Neighbor ID     Pri   State           Dead Time   Address         Interface

blocks.title: R1# show ip route ospf: simulated route excerpt
blocks.text: Authored simulated excerpt. O identifies an intra-area OSPF route. 110 is the conventional Cisco OSPF administrative distance; 11 is this fixture's cost: transit 10 plus remote loopback 1. The next hop is R2's link address, not its router ID. The age is illustrative, not a measured convergence time.

blocks.title: Interpret the route
blocks.text:
Why does the next hop show 10.0.12.2 instead of 2.2.2.2?

Explain your reasoning before opening the answer.
items: 10.0.12.2 is the reachable neighbor interface on the outgoing link. 2.2.2.2 identifies the OSPF router but is not configured as a reachable interface in this fixture. Router identity and packet forwarding address serve different purposes.

inspector.question: Which visible mismatch prevents the intended adjacency?
inspector.answer: Area 1 on R1 versus area 0 on R2. Restore the intended interface area and verify neighbor formation; changing cost alone does not repair an area mismatch.

blocks.title: Failure 1: no neighbor on an up/up link
blocks.text:
Possible causes include OSPF not enabled on the interface, a passive transit interface, area mismatch, incompatible Hello/dead intervals, authentication mismatch, subnet issues, or filtering of protocol 89.

Check show ip interface brief first, then show ip ospf interface GigabitEthernet0/0 on both routers. Compare area, network type, timers, and passive status. An up/up link proves neither OSPF activation nor compatible Hellos.

If R2's transit interface is passive, correct that specific cause:

blocks.title: R2: restore Hello exchanges
blocks.text: Allow time for neighbor formation. Verify Full and the remote loopback route, then test ping 192.168.1.1 source Loopback0 from R2. The source tests the return path to R2's advertised loopback.
items: configure terminal
router ospf 1
no passive-interface GigabitEthernet0/0
end
show ip ospf neighbor
show ip route ospf

blocks.title: Failure 2: ExStart or Exchange persists
blocks.text: Investigate interface MTU mismatch, duplicate router IDs, and exchange problems using show interfaces, show ip ospf, and show ip ospf neighbor detail. Match the intended MTU and correct the actual cause. Do not use ip ospf mtu-ignore as a universal fix; bypassing a check does not repair an underlying data-plane MTU problem.

blocks.title: Failure 3: 2-Way on broadcast Ethernet
blocks.text: First identify roles and network type. Two DROTHERs remaining 2-Way is normal; trying to force every pair to Full is incorrect. The point-to-point fixture above should reach Full, so do not apply the broadcast explanation to it without checking the configuration.

blocks.title: Undo without removing unrelated configuration
blocks.text:
In this isolated fixture, remove interface OSPF activation with no ip ospf 1 area 0 on each participating interface. Remove explicit interface settings with no ip ospf cost and no ip ospf network point-to-point where supported by the stated IOS context.

Only remove the entire process with no router ospf 1 after confirming no other interfaces depend on it. Preserve interface addresses if they serve another exercise. Restore the saved baseline rather than deleting unrelated interfaces.

blocks.title: Mistakes to avoid
blocks.text: Use these checks when the evidence does not fit your first hypothesis.
items: Using a subnet mask instead of a wildcard mask in the 'network' command.
Expecting OSPF process IDs to match between neighbors (they are locally significant).
Expecting DROTHERs to be FULL with each other.
Forgetting that DR election does not preempt; raising priority later has no effect until a re-election.

blocks.title: Choose the correct state interpretation
blocks.text:
Two DROTHERs on one broadcast LAN remain 2-Way. Is the likely conclusion failed MTU negotiation, normal behavior, missing TCP connectivity, or duplicate VLAN IDs?

Explain your reasoning before opening the answer.
items: Normal behavior: DROTHERs form full adjacencies with the DR/BDR, not every other DROTHER. MTU negotiation problems typically affect ExStart/Exchange, not this normal role relationship. OSPF does not require TCP. Duplicate VLAN IDs do not explain the stated neighbor roles.

blocks.title: Calculate the path
blocks.text:
In the stated fixture, is R1's cost to R2's loopback 1, 10, 11, or 110?

Explain your reasoning before opening the answer.
items: 11: add R1's outgoing transit cost 10 and the destination loopback cost 1. 1 omits the transit link. 10 omits the destination stub cost. 110 is Cisco administrative distance, not OSPF path cost.

blocks.title: Distinguish the packet types
blocks.text:
Which carries actual advertisements: DBD, LSR, LSU, or Hello?

Explain your reasoning before opening the answer.
items: LSU carries one or more LSAs. DBD summarizes LSA headers. LSR requests specific advertisements. Hello discovers and maintains neighbors. An LSA is an advertisement inside protocol exchanges, not a sixth OSPF packet type.

blocks.title: Explain it in your own words
blocks.text: OSPFv2 forms adjacencies using Hellos, synchronizes LSDBs, and computes shortest paths with SPF using cost. Know neighbor requirements, states, DR/BDR election, router ID selection, and configuration/verification commands.

blocks.text: Use these as retrieval prompts, not a replacement for the mechanism.
items: Hello 10 s, Dead 40 s (broadcast/P2P). AD 110. Multicast 224.0.0.5 (all) and 224.0.0.6 (DR/BDR).
States: Down, Init, 2-Way, ExStart, Exchange, Loading, Full.
Neighbor must-match: area, subnet, timers, authentication, stub flag; unique RID; MTU for Full.
RID order: manual → highest loopback → highest active interface.
Cost = 100 Mbps / bandwidth (default reference).

items: 2-Way forever because every OSPF link elects a DR
Full, with no DR/BDR election on this network type
ExStart as the final healthy state
Down after the first valid Hello
rationales: Point-to-point links do not use the broadcast DR/BDR adjacency rule.

lessons.title: First Hop Redundancy Protocols
lessons.simple: Hosts usually have only one default gateway configured. If that router fails, they lose access to other networks. A First Hop Redundancy Protocol (FHRP) lets two or more routers share a virtual IP that hosts use as their gateway, so another router takes over automatically.

deep.heading: Virtual gateway
deep.text: Routers R1 (10.1.1.2) and R2 (10.1.1.3) share virtual IP 10.1.1.1 and a virtual MAC. Hosts use 10.1.1.1. One router actively forwards; the other waits.

deep.heading: HSRP, VRRP, GLBP
deep.text: HSRP (Cisco): active/standby routers; default priority 100 (higher wins); preemption disabled by default; virtual MAC 0000.0C07.ACxx (v1) or 0000.0C9F.Fxxx (v2); Hellos to 224.0.0.2 (v1) or 224.0.0.102 (v2). VRRP (IEEE/IETF standard, RFC 5798): master/backup; virtual MAC 0000.5E00.01xx; multicast 224.0.0.18; preemption enabled by default. GLBP (Cisco): one AVG answers ARP with different virtual MACs so multiple AVFs forward simultaneously (load balancing).

deep.heading: What the CCNA expects
deep.text: Objective 3.5 is 'Describe the purpose, functions, and concepts of first hop redundancy protocols'. Be able to explain the virtual IP/MAC concept, failover, and differences between HSRP, VRRP, and GLBP. Basic HSRP syntax for reference: interface Gi0/0 / standby 1 ip 10.1.1.1 / standby 1 priority 110 / standby 1 preempt; verify with 'show standby brief'. When failover occurs, the new active router sends gratuitous ARPs so switches update their MAC tables.

lessons.why: Gateway failure would otherwise isolate an entire VLAN. FHRPs provide sub-second to few-second failover transparent to hosts.

examples.title: Campus VLAN 10
examples.text: Two distribution switches run HSRP for VLAN 10 with virtual IP 10.10.10.1; the left switch is active with priority 110 and preempt.

examples.title: Standards-based
examples.text: A multi-vendor site uses VRRP because HSRP and GLBP are Cisco proprietary.

mistakes: Configuring the virtual IP as one router's physical IP.
Assuming preemption is enabled by default in HSRP.
Thinking HSRP load-balances per host (that is GLBP).

terms.definition: Shared gateway address configured on hosts.
HSRP roles.
VRRP roles.
GLBP Active Virtual Gateway / Active Virtual Forwarder.
Allows a higher-priority router to take over the active role.

memorize: HSRP: Cisco, active/standby, priority 100, no preempt by default, 0000.0C07.ACxx (v1).
VRRP: standard, master/backup, 0000.5E00.01xx, 224.0.0.18.
GLBP: Cisco, load balancing with AVG/AVFs.
examNotes: v1.1 asks you to describe FHRPs (not configure). Focus on concepts and comparisons.

blocks.title: Start with the problem
blocks.text: Hosts can have a perfectly valid default gateway address and still lose remote access when that one router fails. First-hop redundancy gives hosts a stable gateway identity while routers coordinate who forwards for it.

blocks.title: Build the mental model
blocks.text: The host uses a virtual gateway IP and associated virtual MAC. Routers exchange protocol information and select the forwarding role. A surviving router can take over the virtual identity after failure detection. Upstream reachability still matters: an active router with a failed WAN can remain active unless tracking/design causes a change.

lessons.title: DHCP and DNS
lessons.simple: DHCP automatically gives devices their IP address, mask, default gateway, and DNS servers. DNS translates human-friendly names like www.example.com into IP addresses. Together they make networks usable without manual configuration.

deep.heading: DHCP DORA
deep.text: Discover (client broadcast looking for servers), Offer (server proposes an address), Request (client asks for the offered address, broadcast), Acknowledge (server confirms). Clients use UDP 68, servers UDP 67. Leases expire and are renewed.

deep.heading: Cisco IOS DHCP server, relay and client
deep.text: ip dhcp excluded-address 192.168.10.1 192.168.10.10 / ip dhcp pool LAN10 / network 192.168.10.0 255.255.255.0 / default-router 192.168.10.1 / dns-server 8.8.8.8 / lease 7. Because routers do not forward broadcasts, when the server is on another subnet configure a relay on the client-facing gateway interface: 'ip helper-address 10.0.0.50'. The relay converts the broadcast into a unicast to the server and fills in the giaddr field so the server picks the right pool. A router interface can be a DHCP client: 'ip address dhcp'. Verify with 'show ip dhcp binding', 'show ip dhcp pool', 'show ip dhcp conflict'.

deep.heading: DNS
deep.text: DNS uses UDP 53 for standard queries and TCP 53 for zone transfers and large responses. Record types: A (IPv4), AAAA (IPv6), CNAME (alias), MX (mail), PTR (reverse lookup), NS (name server). A client asks its configured resolver; the resolver may query root, TLD, and authoritative servers recursively. On IOS: 'ip name-server 8.8.8.8', 'ip domain-lookup' (default on), 'ip domain-name example.com'; many admins use 'no ip domain-lookup' in labs to stop mistyped commands from being resolved as hostnames.

lessons.why: Almost every endpoint relies on DHCP and DNS. When they fail, users experience 'the internet is down' even though routing works.

examples.text: Branch router Gi0/1 (VLAN 10 gateway) has 'ip helper-address 10.100.1.5' to reach the HQ DHCP server.

Thinking DNS uses only TCP or only UDP.

Gateway function forwarding DHCP broadcasts as unicasts (ip helper-address).

DNS mapping of a name to IPv4 / IPv6 address.

blocks.title: Start with the problem
blocks.text: A new laptop joins a VLAN with no manually entered address. It needs an address, mask, gateway, and resolver before a hostname-based application can work. DHCP supplies configuration; DNS answers naming questions after usable network delivery exists.

blocks.title: Build the mental model
blocks.text: In an initial DHCPv4 allocation, Discover, Offer, Request, and ACK establish a lease. The initial selecting Request is broadcast so servers can see the selection; not every DHCP message in every state is broadcast. Renewals may be unicast. A relay supplies information such as giaddr so the server can select the client subnet. DNS can use UDP or TCP; a hostname lookup is not always one UDP packet.
