blocks.text: Inspect the authored topology and headers step by step.

packet.title: Follow the Packet: DNS, ARP, routing, TCP, HTTP
packet.assumptions: Authored offline walkthrough, not captured traffic or an IOS emulator. IPv4 Ethernet links; no NAT, loss, fragmentation, ACL, or TLS. Client addresses are configured. DNS/gateway cache branches are selectable; router/server ARP caches are prepopulated. Illustrative initial TCP sequences are 1000/5000. MAC addresses are locally administered examples.

devices.name: SW1
devices.details: One VLAN 10: PC-A on Fa0/1, DNS on Fa0/2, R1 on Gi0/1. Forwarding state assumed converged. No routing or NAT.

devices.name: WEB
devices.details: 198.51.100.20/24; gateway 198.51.100.1; MAC 02:00:00:00:20:20; plain HTTP port 80 for this isolated demonstration, not HTTPS.

steps.title: Application requests a hostname
steps.action: The application wants portal.academy.example.
steps.why: It needs an address before selecting a remote transport endpoint.
steps.next: Check the DNS cache.

steps.title: Check DNS cache
steps.action: Inspect the selected cache condition. A warm cache supplies the authored address; a cold cache needs a resolver query.
steps.why: A valid cache entry avoids this resolver exchange, not the later routing and TCP work.
steps.next: For a miss, route to the configured local resolver; for a hit, continue to the web destination.

steps.title: Route to the DNS resolver first
steps.action: 192.168.10.53 is on-link under /24. The resolver MAC is initially unknown.
steps.why: DNS itself needs IP routing and local-link delivery; ARP cannot always wait until after DNS.
steps.next: Broadcast ARP for the resolver.

steps.title: Resolve the local DNS MAC
steps.action: Send an ARP request on VLAN 10. SW1 learns PC-A and floods eligible VLAN 10 ports.
steps.why: The client needs the resolver link address, not the web server MAC.
steps.next: DNS answers the request.

headers.IP header: None: ARP is not an IPv4 packet

steps.title: DNS answers ARP
steps.action: Send a unicast ARP reply; SW1 learns the DNS source MAC.
steps.why: The resolver owns 192.168.10.53 on this link.
steps.next: PC-A can transmit the DNS query.

headers.IP header: None: ARP is not an IPv4 packet

steps.title: Send the DNS query
steps.action: Send a UDP query for an A record.
steps.why: The resolver is local, so the Ethernet destination is DNS, not R1.
steps.next: The authored resolver answers.

steps.title: DNS sends the answer
steps.action: Return the authored A record 198.51.100.20 to PC-A.
steps.why: This example assumes a successful resolver response and omits its upstream work.
steps.next: Route to the web destination.

steps.title: Select the web next hop
steps.why: The IP destination stays the server; the first Ethernet destination must be the local gateway.
steps.next: Use the gateway cache or resolve its MAC.

steps.title: Resolve the gateway
steps.action: Broadcast ARP for 192.168.10.1.
steps.why: The cold gateway-cache branch needs a next-hop MAC.
steps.next: R1 replies.

headers.IP header: None: ARP is not an IPv4 packet

steps.title: R1 answers ARP
steps.action: Reply with the LAN interface MAC.
steps.why: R1 owns the selected next-hop address.
steps.next: The client can send its TCP SYN.

headers.IP header: None: ARP is not an IPv4 packet

steps.title: Inspect remaining assumptions
steps.action: R1/R2 next-hop ARP caches and WEB gateway cache are prepopulated in this authored fixture.
steps.why: This keeps the trace focused without inventing instantaneous unresolved forwarding. Real cold routers would perform their own ARP exchanges.
steps.next: Follow the same SYN across all three Ethernet links.

steps.title: SYN on link 1
steps.action: Transmit the SYN frame. The endpoint creates the segment and IPv4 packet.
steps.why: MAC addresses describe this link. Original IP endpoints and TCP ports are unchanged because no NAT is configured.
steps.next: Inspect the next link or receiving endpoint.

steps.title: SW1 forwards the SYN
steps.action: Forward the known unicast toward R1.
steps.why: SW1 uses VLAN/MAC forwarding and does not decrement IPv4 TTL or replace endpoint MAC addresses.
steps.next: R1 receives and routes the frame.

steps.title: SYN on link 2
steps.action: Transmit the SYN frame. A router has removed the previous Ethernet header, selected the next hop, decremented TTL, and updated the IPv4 header checksum.
steps.why: MAC addresses describe this link. Original IP endpoints and TCP ports are unchanged because no NAT is configured.
steps.next: Inspect the next link or receiving endpoint.

steps.title: SYN on link 3
steps.action: Transmit the SYN frame. A router has removed the previous Ethernet header, selected the next hop, decremented TTL, and updated the IPv4 header checksum.
steps.why: MAC addresses describe this link. Original IP endpoints and TCP ports are unchanged because no NAT is configured.
steps.next: Inspect the next link or receiving endpoint.

steps.title: SYN-ACK on link 1
steps.action: Transmit the SYN-ACK frame. The endpoint creates the segment and IPv4 packet.
steps.why: MAC addresses describe this link. Original IP endpoints and TCP ports are unchanged because no NAT is configured.

blocks.text: Isolated IOS R1 Gi0/0 faces VLAN 10 clients. A preconfigured routed path reaches DHCP server 192.0.2.10, which has a 192.168.10.0/24 scope and a return route. helper-address is placed on the client-facing interface. It does not create a server pool. Undo with no ip helper-address 192.0.2.10 on that interface and restore the prior address. DHCP-client configuration is interface ip address dhcp on a separate intended uplink; do not combine it with this statically addressed client gateway.

Fresh IOS router CLIENT-R1 Gi0/1 connects to a trusted lab DHCP network 192.0.2.0/24. The authorized server has a valid pool, mask, gateway, and DNS options. This is not the statically addressed client-facing relay interface in the earlier example.

blocks.text: interface enters the uplink context. ip address dhcp requests an address rather than assigning a fixed one. no shutdown enables the link. The server decides the lease/options; the client command does not create a pool. show dhcp lease is a supported IOS DHCP-client inspection command on applicable releases; use the platform equivalent if absent.

blocks.title: What evidence should show
blocks.text: Inspect client lease details and resolver settings. On IOS relay R1 inspect show running-config interface GigabitEthernet0/0 and routes to the server. On a client use nslookup portal.academy.example against the intended resolver. A valid lease proves configuration delivery, not DNS or application success.

blocks.title: IOS DHCP client on a separate uplink | verification and expected result
blocks.text: Expect an assigned address within the authorized pool, not a fixed invented value. Verify lease details, interface state, installed routes, and resolver settings. A lease alone does not prove remote application access.

blocks.title: Diagnose, correct, and retest
blocks.text: If Discover repeats with no Offer, inspect VLAN, relay, server scope, routing, and snooping policy. If an address is assigned but names fail, inspect DNS separately. Correct the evidenced relay/scope/resolver issue, renew only the test client if appropriate, and retest the original hostname/application.

blocks.title: Mistakes to avoid
blocks.text: Use these checks when the evidence does not fit your first hypothesis.
items: Placing 'ip helper-address' on the server-facing interface instead of the client-facing interface.
Forgetting to exclude gateway and server addresses from the pool.
Thinking DNS uses only TCP or only UDP.

blocks.title: IOS DHCP client on a separate uplink | correction and safe restoration
blocks.text: If no lease arrives, inspect link/VLAN, server scope, relay if needed, and DHCP filtering. Restore the original static or DHCP addressing through console access. Removing ip address dhcp can immediately remove management reachability; do not do it on an active remote management path.

blocks.title: Apply the idea
blocks.text: A client has a valid lease and can reach a server by IP but not by name. Which service is the focused next check?
items: Re-run every DHCP allocation indefinitely
Change all VLAN IDs
Disable ARP
DNS
rationales: A working lease does not justify repeatedly restarting allocation.
Changing VLANs can disrupt a working IP path without addressing the resolver.
ARP supports local delivery and disabling it is not a DNS repair.
Name resolution is the distinguishing failed function.

lessons.title: NAT and PAT
lessons.simple: NAT translates private inside addresses to public addresses as traffic leaves the network. PAT (NAT overload) lets thousands of inside devices share a single public IP by tracking each connection's port number.

deep.heading: Why NAT exists
deep.text: Public IPv4 addresses are scarce. Organizations use private RFC 1918 addresses internally and translate them at the internet edge.

deep.heading: The four address terms
deep.text: Inside local: the inside host's real (usually private) address. Inside global: the public address representing the inside host. Outside local: the outside host's address as seen from inside (usually same as outside global). Outside global: the outside host's real public address. Mark interfaces with 'ip nat inside' and 'ip nat outside'.

deep.heading: Static NAT, dynamic NAT, and PAT configuration
deep.text: Static (one-to-one, permanent, allows inbound connections): ip nat inside source static 192.168.1.10 203.0.113.10. Dynamic (pool, one-to-one while in use): access-list 1 permit 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255 / ip nat pool PUB 203.0.113.20 203.0.113.30 netmask 255.255.255.0 / ip nat inside source list 1 pool PUB. If the pool is exhausted, new hosts fail. PAT: ip nat inside source list 1 interface GigabitEthernet0/1 overload (or 'pool PUB overload'). Verify with 'show ip nat translations' and 'show ip nat statistics'; clear dynamic entries with 'clear ip nat translation *'. Debug with 'debug ip nat'.

lessons.why: Nearly every internet-connected network uses PAT. Understanding NAT terms is essential for reading translation tables and troubleshooting.

examples.title: Home/office PAT
examples.text: 192.168.1.10:51000 and 192.168.1.11:51000 both leave as 203.0.113.2, with PAT assigning unique source ports (e.g., 51000 and 51001) to keep them apart.

examples.text: Static NAT maps web server 192.168.1.10 to 203.0.113.10 so internet users can reach it.

ACL used for NAT not matching the inside subnet.

blocks.title: Start with the problem
blocks.text: A private-addressed branch needs to communicate with an external network that does not route its internal addresses. NAT changes selected address fields at a boundary; routing still chooses paths and security policy still decides what is permitted.

blocks.title: Build the mental model
blocks.text: Inside local is the inside host address as seen internally; inside global is its translated external representation. Outside local/global describe the outside host from the respective views. For basic inside-source translation, an outbound source is rewritten and return traffic is translated back. Checksums must reflect changed fields. This is the explicit exception to ordinary routing preserving IP endpoints.

blocks.title: Follow the behavior
blocks.text:
1. Inside host 192.168.10.10 sends toward an external lab server.
2. R1 matches its static mapping to 198.51.100.10.
3. The outbound source becomes 198.51.100.10.
4. The external network routes replies to that address.
5. R1 translates the reply destination back to 192.168.10.10.
6. Layer 2 headers are independently rebuilt on each routed link.

blocks.title: Dynamic NAT pool without overload | command purpose and modes
blocks.text: Interface commands identify inside/outside roles. The standard ACL selects inside source addresses for translation; it is not applied as an interface firewall. ip nat pool defines eleven usable global addresses. The final source-list command binds selection to the pool. Without overload, simultaneous inside hosts consume one-to-one mappings; pool exhaustion can prevent new allocations.

blocks.text: The ACL selects inside sources. interface GigabitEthernet0/1 chooses its address as the global representation. overload permits multiple flows to share it using transport identifiers. blocks.text: Use show ip nat translations and show ip nat statistics on a NAT-capable IOS router. Inspect inside local/global, protocol/ports where relevant, interface roles, and counters. A static mapping can exist before traffic. For dynamic NAT, generate matching traffic and verify pool availability and routes.

blocks.title: Dynamic NAT pool without overload | verification and expected result
blocks.text: Generate approved inside-originated traffic and inspect inside local/global mappings and pool use. Expect globals within .10-.20; do not assume one predetermined allocation order. Verify return routing to the pool. These are expectations, not live outputs.

blocks.title: PAT as a separate alternative | verification and expected result
blocks.text: Generate two inside TCP/UDP flows and inspect distinct translation tuples sharing the interface global address. A PAT mapping does not encrypt data or automatically permit unsolicited inbound services.

blocks.title: Diagnose, correct, and retest
blocks.text: If no dynamic translation appears, check inside/outside roles, matching ACL, route, and pool availability. If a translation exists but replies fail, inspect external routing to the global address and return policy. Correct the specific issue and retest the same inside-originated flow. Clearing all translations can disrupt unrelated sessions.

lessons.title: NTP, SNMP, and Syslog
lessons.simple: Network management relies on three services: NTP keeps every device's clock accurate, SNMP lets monitoring systems read and change device information, and Syslog sends event messages to a central server. Accurate time makes logs meaningful.

deep.heading: NTP
deep.text: NTP synchronizes clocks over UDP 123. Stratum indicates distance from an authoritative source: stratum 0 is a reference clock (GPS/atomic), stratum 1 servers connect to it, and so on (lower is more accurate). Configure a client: 'ntp server 192.0.2.1'. Make a router an NTP server: 'ntp master 4' (or simply have it synchronized and serving). Verify: 'show ntp status', 'show ntp associations'; set display time zone with 'clock timezone'.

deep.heading: SNMP
deep.text: An SNMP manager (NMS) polls agents on devices using UDP 161; agents send unsolicited Traps or Informs (acknowledged) to the manager on UDP 162. Data is organized in the MIB and identified by OIDs. Operations: Get, GetNext, GetBulk (v2c+), Set, Trap, Inform. SNMPv1/v2c use community strings sent in clear text (read-only/read-write). SNMPv3 adds users with security levels noAuthNoPriv, authNoPriv, and authPriv (authentication and encryption).

deep.heading: Syslog
deep.text: Messages look like '%LINEPROTO-5-UPDOWN: Line protocol on Interface Gi0/1, changed state to down' — facility (LINEPROTO), severity (5), mnemonic (UPDOWN), description. Severities: 0 Emergency, 1 Alert, 2 Critical, 3 Error, 4 Warning, 5 Notification, 6 Informational, 7 Debugging (mnemonic: 'Every Awesome Cisco Engineer Will Need Ice cream Daily'). A configured level includes that level and all more severe (lower numbers). Destinations: console ('logging console'), buffer ('logging buffered'), terminal lines ('terminal monitor' for VTY), and servers ('logging host 192.0.2.50', 'logging trap warnings'). Syslog uses UDP 514. Add timestamps with 'service timestamps log datetime msec'.

lessons.why: Without accurate time and centralized logs, you cannot correlate events across devices, investigate incidents, or meet audit requirements.

examples.title: Logging level
examples.text: 'logging trap 4' sends levels 0-4 (Emergency to Warning) to the syslog server; Notification (5) messages are not sent.

examples.title: SNMP monitoring
examples.text: An NMS polls interface counters every 5 minutes via SNMP Get and receives a Trap when a link goes down.

mistakes: Thinking 'logging trap 4' sends level 4 and higher numbers; it sends 4 and lower numbers (more severe).
Confusing SNMP agent port 161 with trap port 162.
Expecting SNMPv2c to encrypt community strings.
Forgetting that 'terminal monitor' is needed to see logs in an SSH session.

terms.definition: NTP distance from the reference clock.
SNMP Management Information Base / Object Identifier.
Unsolicited SNMP notification; Inform is acknowledged.
Syslog source category, e.g., LINK, OSPF, SYS.

memorize: NTP UDP 123; SNMP UDP 161 (polls) and 162 (traps/informs); Syslog UDP 514.
Syslog levels 0-7: Emergency, Alert, Critical, Error, Warning, Notification, Informational, Debugging.
SNMPv3 authPriv = authentication + encryption.
Logging a level includes all more severe levels.
examNotes: Expect to decode a syslog message and identify its severity level and meaning.
Know SNMP message types and which direction they flow.
lessons.summary: NTP keeps clocks synchronized by stratum, SNMP polls (161) and receives traps (162) using MIBs/OIDs with v3 adding security, and Syslog sends graded messages (0-7) to local and remote destinations.

blocks.title: Start with the problem
blocks.text: Three routers report the same outage at different times, and monitoring shows a spike without an explanation. Operations needs a shared clock, measurable counters, and event messages. NTP, SNMP, and syslog supply different pieces of that evidence.

blocks.title: Build the mental model
blocks.text: NTP clients evaluate time sources; stratum describes distance from a reference, not a guarantee of accuracy or trust. SNMP managers query agents using MIB object identifiers; counters often require time deltas to become rates. SNMPv3 security capabilities differ from community-based versions. Syslog delivery and retention depend on transport, filtering, and collector configuration.

Destinations: console ('logging console'), buffer ('logging buffered'), terminal lines ('terminal monitor' for VTY), and servers ('logging host 192.0.2.50', 'logging trap warnings'). Syslog uses UDP 514. Add timestamps with 'service timestamps log datetime msec'.

blocks.text: NTP synchronizes time; SNMP reads/manages structured objects and can notify; syslog sends event messages with facilities and severity. A syslog severity number is not an SNMP OID. Lower syslog severity numbers mean more severe events, from emergency 0 through debugging 7.

1. R1 exchanges time information with its configured source.
2. A manager polls an interface counter twice and calculates a delta over elapsed time.
3. A link-state change produces a syslog message if enabled and within the threshold.
4. The collector timestamps/correlates evidence.
5. A missing message can reflect filtering or delivery failure, not absence of an event.

IOS R1 10.0.12.1/30 and R2 10.0.12.2/30 share a working link. R1 has no external source in this deliberately isolated lab. The local-master example is not an accurate UTC reference and must not be advertised to production.

end

Informational level 6
Emergency level 0
Critical level 2

6 is numerically above the configured threshold.
0 is included and is the most severe level.
2 is included.

lessons.title: Quality of Service (QoS)
lessons.simple: QoS decides which traffic goes first when a link is congested. Voice and video are sensitive to delay, so they get priority, while bulk downloads can wait. QoS does not create bandwidth; it manages it.

deep.heading: What hurts real-time traffic
deep.text: Bandwidth (capacity), delay/latency (time to arrive), jitter (variation in delay), and loss (dropped packets). Cisco guidance for voice: one-way delay ≤ 150 ms, jitter ≤ 30 ms, loss ≤ 1%.

deep.heading: Classification and marking
deep.text: Classification identifies traffic (by ACL, NBAR, or existing markings). Marking writes a value into the header so other devices can act on it: Layer 2 CoS (3 bits in the 802.1Q PCP field, 0-7); Layer 3 DSCP (6 bits in the IP header's ToS/Traffic Class byte, 0-63). Common DSCP values: EF (46) for voice, AF classes (AF41 for video, etc.), CS values. A trust boundary is where markings start being trusted, ideally at the IP phone or access switch.

deep.heading: Queuing, congestion avoidance, policing and shaping
deep.text: Queuing schedules packets when an interface is congested: CBWFQ guarantees bandwidth per class; LLQ adds a strict priority queue for voice (with a policer to prevent starvation of other queues). Congestion avoidance: tail drop discards new packets when the queue is full, causing TCP global synchronization; WRED randomly drops lower-priority packets earlier to avoid that. Policing enforces a rate by dropping or re-marking excess traffic (no buffering; ingress or egress, common at provider edges). Shaping buffers excess traffic and sends it later (egress only, adds delay, common on the customer side to match a provider's policed rate).

lessons.why: Converged networks carry voice, video, and data on one infrastructure. Without QoS, a large download can make a phone call unusable.

examples.title: Branch WAN
examples.text: Voice marked EF is placed in an LLQ priority queue; business apps get CBWFQ guarantees; everything else is best effort.

examples.title: Provider contract
examples.text: A 1 Gbps circuit is policed by the ISP to 200 Mbps; the customer shapes outbound traffic to 200 Mbps to avoid drops.

mistakes: Thinking QoS adds bandwidth.
Confusing policing (drop/re-mark, no delay) with shaping (buffer, adds delay).
Mixing up CoS (Layer 2, 3 bits) and DSCP (Layer 3, 6 bits).

terms.definition: Differentiated Services Code Point, 6-bit Layer 3 marking.
Class of Service, 3-bit Layer 2 marking in 802.1Q.
Low Latency Queuing: strict priority queue plus CBWFQ.
Weighted Random Early Detection congestion avoidance.
Point where QoS markings are accepted as valid.

memorize: Voice: delay ≤150 ms, jitter ≤30 ms, loss ≤1%; EF = DSCP 46.
Policing drops/re-marks; shaping buffers (egress only).
LLQ = priority queue for voice; WRED avoids TCP global synchronization.

blocks.text: A backup transfer fills a WAN uplink and voice becomes choppy. QoS cannot create more bandwidth, but it can classify traffic and decide how limited forwarding resources are shared when congestion occurs.

blocks.title: Build the mental model
blocks.text: Congestion occurs when offered traffic exceeds a resource's service capacity. Delay, jitter, and loss affect applications differently. Priority treatment must be bounded so other traffic is not starved. Trust boundaries determine whose markings are accepted; accepting every endpoint's highest-priority mark defeats policy.

lessons.title: Security Concepts and Security Program Elements
lessons.simple: Security is about protecting confidentiality, integrity, and availability (the CIA triad). You need to understand what threatens a network, how weaknesses get exploited, and which policies and training reduce risk.

deep.heading: Core vocabulary
deep.text: A vulnerability is a weakness. A threat is a potential danger that could exploit it. An exploit is the actual method or code used to take advantage of a vulnerability. Mitigation is the action that reduces the risk.

deep.heading: Common attacks
deep.text: DoS/DDoS (overwhelm resources), spoofing (fake IP/MAC/ARP/DHCP identity), reflection and amplification (spoof the victim's address so responses flood it), man-in-the-middle (intercept traffic, e.g., ARP poisoning), reconnaissance (scanning to gather information), malware (virus needs a host file and user action, worm self-propagates, trojan disguises itself, ransomware encrypts data for ransom), social engineering (phishing, spear phishing, whaling, vishing by voice, smishing by SMS, pretexting, tailgating), and password attacks (dictionary, brute force).

deep.heading: Security program elements
deep.text: User awareness (making everyone aware of threats and policies, e.g., phishing simulations), user training (formal instruction for specific roles), and physical access control (badges, locks, cameras, mantraps protecting network rooms). Technical controls are useless if anyone can walk into the wiring closet and plug in a console cable.

lessons.why: Most breaches begin with people or simple misconfigurations, not sophisticated exploits. CCNA-level engineers are the first line of defense.

examples.title: Phishing
examples.text: An email impersonating IT asks users to 'verify' passwords on a fake portal. Awareness training and MFA reduce the impact.

examples.title: Amplification
examples.text: Attackers send small spoofed DNS queries; large responses flood the victim.

mistakes: Using 'threat' and 'vulnerability' interchangeably.
Thinking a worm needs user action to spread.
Neglecting physical security.

terms.definition: Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability.
Mechanism that takes advantage of a vulnerability.
Man-in-the-middle: attacker intercepts and possibly alters traffic.
Targeted phishing / phishing aimed at executives.

memorize: Vulnerability = weakness; threat = potential danger; exploit = the attack method; mitigation = the countermeasure.
Program elements: user awareness, user training, physical access control.

Awareness training helps users recognize suspicious requests, while patching and access controls reduce technical exposure. A control can reduce likelihood or impact without eliminating every threat.

lessons.title: Device Access Control, Passwords, and AAA
lessons.simple: Every router and switch must be protected so only authorized administrators can log in, and their actions should be controlled and recorded. Strong password policies, multifactor authentication, and AAA with central servers make that possible.

deep.heading: Local passwords
deep.text: Console: line console 0 / password X / login. VTY: line vty 0 4 / password X / login (or 'login local' with usernames). Privileged EXEC: 'enable secret X' (hashed; preferred over 'enable password', and if both exist, enable secret is used). 'username admin secret X' creates a local user with a hashed password. 'service password-encryption' applies weak type 7 encryption to clear-text passwords in the config; it only prevents shoulder-surfing.

deep.heading: Password policies and alternatives
deep.text: Policies cover length, complexity, expiration, reuse, and lockout ('login block-for 120 attempts 3 within 60'). Alternatives and additions: multifactor authentication (MFA) combining something you know, have, and are; digital certificates (PKI) proving identity cryptographically; biometrics (fingerprint, face). Also set 'exec-timeout' to log out idle sessions.

deep.heading: AAA, RADIUS, and TACACS+
deep.text: Authentication (who are you), Authorization (what may you do), Accounting (what did you do). Enable with 'aaa new-model'. RADIUS: open standard, UDP 1812/1813 (legacy 1645/1646), encrypts only the password, combines authentication and authorization; common for network access (802.1X, VPN users). TACACS+: Cisco-developed, TCP 49, encrypts the entire payload, separates all three A's, supports per-command authorization; preferred for device administration. Cisco ISE can act as both. Always keep a local fallback: 'aaa authentication login default group tacacs+ local'.

lessons.why: Compromised device credentials give an attacker the whole network. AAA provides accountability and centralized control over who changes what.

examples.title: Secure login
examples.text: enable secret, local users with secret, login local on VTY, SSH only, exec-timeout 10, login block-for to slow brute force.

examples.title: Central admin
examples.text: All switches authenticate administrators via TACACS+ on ISE; helpdesk staff are authorized only for show commands; every command is logged by accounting.

mistakes: Using 'enable password' instead of 'enable secret'.
Believing 'service password-encryption' is strong encryption.
Configuring AAA without a local fallback and locking yourself out.
Mixing up RADIUS (UDP) and TACACS+ (TCP 49).

terms.definition: Authentication, Authorization, Accounting.
Standard AAA protocol, UDP 1812/1813, encrypts password only.
Cisco AAA protocol, TCP 49, full-payload encryption.
Multifactor authentication using two or more factor types.

memorize: enable secret beats enable password; type 7 is reversible.
RADIUS: UDP 1812/1813, password-only encryption, combines authN/authZ.
TACACS+: TCP 49, full encryption, separates AAA, per-command authorization.
MFA factors: know, have, are.
examNotes: Comparison tables of RADIUS vs TACACS+ are very common.
lessons.summary: Protect device access with hashed secrets, local users, and timeouts; strengthen authentication with password policy, MFA, certificates, or biometrics; and centralize control with AAA using RADIUS or TACACS+.

items: Every router and switch must be protected so only authorized administrators can log in, and their actions should be controlled and recorded. Strong password policies, multifactor authentication, and AAA with central servers make that possible.

blocks.title: Why this matters in practice
blocks.text: Open this explanation when you are ready for the full mechanism.
items: Compromised device credentials give an attacker the whole network. AAA provides accountability and centralized control over who changes what.

blocks.title: Local passwords
blocks.text: Open this explanation when you are ready for the full mechanism.
items: Console: line console 0 / password X / login. VTY: line vty 0 4 / password X / login (or 'login local' with usernames). Privileged EXEC: 'enable secret X' (hashed; preferred over 'enable password', and if both exist, enable secret is used). 'username admin secret X' creates a local user with a hashed password. 'service password-encryption' applies weak type 7 encryption to clear-text passwords in the config; it only prevents shoulder-surfing.

blocks.title: Password policies and alternatives
blocks.text: Open this explanation when you are ready for the full mechanism.
items: Policies cover length, complexity, expiration, reuse, and lockout ('login block-for 120 attempts 3 within 60'). Alternatives and additions: multifactor authentication (MFA) combining something you know, have, and are; digital certificates (PKI) proving identity cryptographically; biometrics (fingerprint, face). Also set 'exec-timeout' to log out idle sessions.

blocks.title: AAA, RADIUS, and TACACS+
blocks.text: Open this explanation when you are ready for the full mechanism.
items: Authentication (who are you), Authorization (what may you do), Accounting (what did you do). Enable with 'aaa new-model'. RADIUS: open standard, UDP 1812/1813 (legacy 1645/1646), encrypts only the password, combines authentication and authorization; common for network access (802.1X, VPN users). TACACS+: Cisco-developed, TCP 49, encrypts the entire payload, separates all three A's, supports per-command authorization; preferred for device administration. Cisco ISE can act as both. Always keep a local fallback: 'aaa authentication login default group tacacs+ local'.

blocks.title: Separate the similar ideas
blocks.text: Authentication asks who you are; authorization asks what you may do; accounting records activity. A local user database is different from centralized TACACS+/RADIUS. A password policy, MFA, certificates, and biometrics address identity assurance in different ways; a long password alone does not replace every other control.

blocks.title: Read the relationships
blocks.text: Place three checkpoints along a management session: identity, permission, audit record. Keep the encrypted SSH transport around the conversation as a separate layer. A secure transport does not automatically grant the correct privilege.

blocks.title: Follow the behavior
blocks.text:
1. A user connects over an allowed management path.
2. The configured authentication method validates identity.
3. Authorization limits commands/roles.
4. Accounting records supported actions.
5. A centralized server timeout may invoke a configured fallback; an explicit rejection is not the same as an unreachable server.

blocks.title: Secure login
blocks.text: Open this explanation when you are ready for the full mechanism.
items: enable secret, local users with secret, login local on VTY, SSH only, exec-timeout 10, login block-for to slow brute force.

blocks.title: Central admin
blocks.text: Open this explanation when you are ready for the full mechanism.
items: All switches authenticate administrators via TACACS+ on ISE; helpdesk staff are authorized only for show commands; every command is logged by accounting.

blocks.title: Fixture, command context, and restoration
blocks.text: Isolated IOS lab with existing privileged recovery access and no conflicting AAA method-list policy. The disposable password is not a production credential. username creates a local low-privilege account; line console selects console configuration; login local uses that database. This does not configure SSH or centralized AAA. Before closing recovery access, test the intended login and privilege behavior. Undo by restoring the prior console authentication and removing only the lab user; never leave a production console unauthenticated.

blocks.text: Use authorized console access to inspect local users, enable secret, line authentication, and configured AAA method lists. Test with a low-privilege account and a separate recovery path. show users identifies sessions but does not prove that every action is being accounted for.

blocks.title: Diagnose, correct, and retest
blocks.text: If login fails after an AAA change, distinguish server reachability from credential rejection. Do not remove all authentication on a remotely managed device. Restore the approved method list via recovery access, verify both authorized and unauthorized test cases, and preserve accounting evidence.

items: Using 'enable password' instead of 'enable secret'.
Believing 'service password-encryption' is strong encryption.

Mixing up RADIUS (UDP) and TACACS+ (TCP 49).

items: Accounting only
Ethernet learning
Authorization

rationales: Accounting records activity rather than granting the command.
MAC learning is unrelated to management permissions.
Authorization determines permitted actions.

blocks.title: Explain it in your own words
blocks.text: Protect device access with hashed secrets, local users, and timeouts; strengthen authentication with password policy, MFA, certificates, or biometrics; and centralize control with AAA using RADIUS or TACACS+.

RADIUS: UDP 1812/1813, password-only encryption, combines authN/authZ.

lessons.title: Access Control Lists (ACLs)
lessons.simple: An ACL is an ordered list of permit and deny rules. Routers use ACLs to filter traffic on interfaces and to identify traffic for features like NAT. Every packet is checked against the list top to bottom; the first match decides.

deep.heading: How ACLs evaluate
deep.text: Rules are checked in order. The first matching rule's action is applied and no more rules are checked. If nothing matches, the invisible implicit 'deny any' at the end drops the packet. An ACL with only deny statements therefore blocks everything.

deep.heading: Standard vs extended, and wildcard masks
deep.text: Standard ACLs (1-99, 1300-1999) match only the source IP. Extended ACLs (100-199, 2000-2699) match protocol, source, destination, and ports. Named ACLs work the same way with names. Wildcard masks use 0 = must match, 1 = ignore: 0.0.0.255 matches a /24; 'host 10.1.1.1' = 10.1.1.1 0.0.0.0; 'any' = 0.0.0.0 255.255.255.255. Wildcard for a subnet = 255.255.255.255 - subnet mask (e.g., /26 → 0.0.0.63).

deep.heading: Configuration, placement and verification
deep.text: Numbered standard: access-list 10 permit 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255. Named extended: ip access-list extended WEB / 10 permit tcp 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.2.2.10 eq 443 / 20 deny ip any host 10.2.2.10 / 30 permit ip any any. Apply: interface Gi0/1 / ip access-group WEB in. Rules: one ACL per interface, per direction, per protocol (IPv4/IPv6). Place extended ACLs close to the source (drop unwanted traffic early); place standard ACLs close to the destination (they cannot distinguish destinations). Named ACLs allow inserting/deleting individual sequence numbers. Restrict VTY access with 'access-class 5 in' under line vty. Verify: 'show access-lists' (with match counters), 'show ip interface Gi0/1'.

lessons.why: ACLs are the most common packet-filtering and traffic-identification tool on Cisco devices and appear in many exam scenarios.

examples.title: Block one host from a server
examples.text: ip access-list extended BLOCK / deny ip host 10.1.1.50 host 10.2.2.10 / permit ip any any — applied inbound on the interface closest to 10.1.1.50.

lessons.title: Layer 2 Security: Port Security, DHCP Snooping, and DAI
lessons.simple: Attacks inside the LAN often target Layer 2: plugging in unauthorized devices, running rogue DHCP servers, or poisoning ARP caches. Port security, DHCP snooping, and Dynamic ARP Inspection stop these attacks at the access switch.

deep.heading: Port security
deep.text: Limits which and how many MAC addresses can use a port. Enable on an access (or static trunk) port: switchport mode access / switchport port-security / switchport port-security maximum 2 / switchport port-security mac-address sticky. Default maximum is 1 MAC and default violation mode is shutdown.

deep.heading: Violation modes and recovery
deep.text: Shutdown: port goes err-disabled, increments violation counter, sends log/SNMP (default). Restrict: drops offending frames, logs, increments counter. Protect: drops offending frames silently (no log, no counter). Recover from err-disabled with 'shutdown' then 'no shutdown' or automatically with 'errdisable recovery cause psecure-violation'. Verify: 'show port-security interface Gi0/5', 'show port-security address'. Sticky addresses are added to the running config.

deep.heading: DHCP snooping and DAI
deep.text: DHCP snooping ('ip dhcp snooping', 'ip dhcp snooping vlan 10') classifies ports as trusted (uplinks toward legitimate DHCP servers: 'ip dhcp snooping trust') or untrusted (default). Untrusted ports drop DHCP server messages (OFFER, ACK, NAK), blocking rogue servers, and the switch builds a binding table (MAC, IP, VLAN, port, lease). Optional rate limiting: 'ip dhcp snooping limit rate 10'. Note: when snooping inserts Option 82, some IOS DHCP servers reject it; 'no ip dhcp snooping information option' is a common fix. Dynamic ARP Inspection ('ip arp inspection vlan 10') checks ARP messages on untrusted ports against the DHCP snooping binding table (or ARP ACLs for static hosts) and drops mismatches, preventing ARP spoofing/poisoning. Trust uplinks with 'ip arp inspection trust'. Untrusted ports are rate limited to 15 ARP packets per second by default. Optional 'ip arp inspection validate src-mac dst-mac ip'.

lessons.why: These features stop common, easy LAN attacks such as rogue DHCP servers (traffic redirection) and ARP poisoning (man-in-the-middle).

examples.title: Conference room port
examples.text: maximum 1, sticky, violation restrict: a visitor's laptop is blocked and logged without shutting the port.

examples.title: Rogue DHCP
examples.text: A user plugs in a home router. DHCP snooping drops its OFFERs on the untrusted port; clients still get addresses from the real server via the trusted uplink.

mistakes: Enabling DAI without DHCP snooping (DAI needs the binding table or ARP ACLs).
Forgetting to trust the uplink toward the DHCP server, so all clients fail.
Enabling port security on a dynamic (DTP) port — IOS rejects it.
Mixing up protect (silent) and restrict (logs).

terms.definition: Port state disabled by the switch due to an error/violation.
Dynamically learned MAC saved into the running configuration.
DHCP snooping record of MAC, IP, VLAN, interface, lease.
Sending false ARP replies to redirect traffic.

memorize: Port security defaults: max 1, violation shutdown.
Modes: protect (drop silently), restrict (drop + log + counter), shutdown (err-disable).
DHCP snooping: untrusted ports drop server messages; trust uplinks.
DAI uses the DHCP snooping binding table; default 15 pps limit on untrusted ports.
examNotes: Expect a 'show port-security interface' output and questions about the violation mode or counter.
lessons.summary: Port security restricts MAC addresses per port, DHCP snooping blocks rogue DHCP servers and builds a binding table, and DAI uses that table to stop ARP spoofing.

quiz.explanation: Server-originated messages such as OFFER/ACK/NAK are dropped.

blocks.text:
Isolated Catalyst IOS switch SW1 Fa0/1 connects to exactly one authorized PC in VLAN 10. No phone, AP, hypervisor, or downstream switch shares the port. Capture the original policy and MAC evidence before enabling sticky learning.

Instructional configuration for an isolated lab, not a live connection. Unsupported commands must not be entered into the offline trainer as if it were full IOS.

blocks.title: Port security on one endpoint port | configuration
blocks.text: Copy only into the stated device/context after capturing its baseline.
items: enable
configure terminal
interface FastEthernet0/1
switchport mode access
switchport access vlan 10
switchport port-security
switchport port-security maximum 1
switchport port-security violation restrict
switchport port-security mac-address sticky
end
show port-security interface FastEthernet0/1
show port-security address

blocks.title: Port security on one endpoint port | command purpose and modes
blocks.text: Port security requires a supported static access-port context here. maximum 1 permits one secure MAC; restrict drops violating traffic and reports supported violation evidence rather than using the shutdown mode. Sticky learning records learned secure addresses in running configuration; saving configuration affects persistence. Learn only from the intended endpoint, not an unknown device.

blocks.title: DAI with DHCP clients and one static printer | objective and fixture
blocks.text:
SW1 VLAN 10: Fa0/1 DHCP PC, Fa0/2 static printer 192.168.10.50 MAC 0200.0000.1050. Gi0/1 leads only to authorized gateway/DHCP infrastructure. DHCP snooping is already enabled on VLAN 10, Gi0/1 is snooping-trusted, and the PC binding has been verified. Plan persistence/rate limits before enforcement.

Instructional configuration for an isolated lab, not a live connection. Unsupported commands must not be entered into the offline trainer as if it were full IOS.

blocks.title: DAI with DHCP clients and one static printer | configuration
blocks.text: Copy only into the stated device/context after capturing its baseline.
items: enable
configure terminal
arp access-list ACADEMY_STATIC
permit ip host 192.168.10.50 mac host 0200.0000.1050
exit
ip arp inspection filter ACADEMY_STATIC vlan 10
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
ip arp inspection trust
exit
ip arp inspection vlan 10
end
show ip arp inspection vlan 10
show ip arp inspection interfaces
show arp access-list ACADEMY_STATIC

blocks.title: DAI with DHCP clients and one static printer | command purpose and modes
blocks.text: arp access-list enters ARP ACL mode; the permit validates the printer sender binding. filter applies that ACL to VLAN 10. The static keyword is deliberately omitted so unmatched packets can fall back to DHCP snooping bindings; using static would change that behavior. DAI trust is separate from DHCP-snooping trust. Enabling the VLAN starts ingress inspection on untrusted ports.

blocks.title: What evidence should show
blocks.text: Use show ip dhcp snooping, show ip dhcp snooping binding, show ip arp inspection vlan 10, and show port-security interface FastEthernet0/1 on supported Catalyst IOS. Check enabled VLANs, trusted interfaces, actual bindings, drop counters, and violation mode. Do not enable DAI before planning static-host handling and binding persistence.

blocks.title: Port security on one endpoint port | verification and expected result
blocks.text: Generate legitimate traffic, inspect the secure MAC and port, then test an approved alternate endpoint in the isolated lab. Expect violation/drop evidence under restrict, not an automatic claim that the port is err-disabled. Review the actual platform output and counters.

blocks.title: DAI with DHCP clients and one static printer | verification and expected result
blocks.text: Check PC binding, static printer policy, trusted uplink, and DAI counters. Legitimate DHCP-client and printer ARP should pass; an unauthorized mapping should be rejected in an approved isolated test. Do not invent a universal default rate: inspect the platform and configure a justified limit if required.

blocks.title: Diagnose, correct, and retest
blocks.text: After DAI is enabled, a static printer fails while DHCP clients work. Inspect missing binding/ARP ACL coverage before trusting every access port. Add a validated static-host policy through the platform-supported method, then test legitimate ARP and rejection of an unauthorized mapping. If a port is err-disabled, remove the cause before recovery.

blocks.title: Mistakes to avoid
blocks.text: Use these checks when the evidence does not fit your first hypothesis.
items: Enabling DAI without DHCP snooping (DAI needs the binding table or ARP ACLs).
Forgetting to trust the uplink toward the DHCP server, so all clients fail.
Enabling port security on a dynamic (DTP) port — IOS rejects it.
Mixing up protect (silent) and restrict (logs).

blocks.title: Port security on one endpoint port | correction and safe restoration
blocks.text: If a legitimate replacement PC fails, compare the secure MAC with the approved inventory. Remove/replace only the stale secure entry through the supported command, then retest. Undo the lab port-security settings and any generated sticky lines from the captured baseline; disabling the feature does not justify leaving stale saved configuration unreviewed.

blocks.title: DAI with DHCP clients and one static printer | correction and safe restoration
blocks.text: If the printer fails, verify exact sender IP/MAC and ACL application. If all clients fail after reload, inspect binding persistence before bypassing inspection. In the lab, remove the VLAN enforcement and filter only through a planned restoration, then remove the unused ACL and restore trust policy. Never trust all access ports as a generic repair.

blocks.title: Apply the idea
blocks.text: A static printer has no DHCP snooping binding. What is the safest design response before enforcing DAI?
items: Plan validated static-host ARP policy
Trust every client port
Assume DAI creates a lease automatically
Disable all switch security permanently
rationales: Static devices need explicit validated treatment such as an appropriate ARP ACL.
Blanket trust bypasses the intended checks.
DAI does not act as a DHCP server.
Removing all protection is not a targeted solution.

blocks.title: Explain it in your own words
blocks.text: Port security restricts MAC addresses per port, DHCP snooping blocks rogue DHCP servers and builds a binding table, and DAI uses that table to stop ARP spoofing.

blocks.title: Facts worth retrieving from memory
blocks.text: Use these as retrieval prompts, not a replacement for the mechanism.
items: Port security defaults: max 1, violation shutdown.
Modes: protect (drop silently), restrict (drop + log + counter), shutdown (err-disable).
DHCP snooping: untrusted ports drop server messages; trust uplinks.
DAI uses the DHCP snooping binding table; default 15 pps limit on untrusted ports.

blocks.title: Exam interpretation
blocks.text: Original objective-linked exam notes are retained.
items: Expect a 'show port-security interface' output and questions about the violation mode or counter.

lessons.title: VPN Fundamentals
lessons.simple: A VPN creates a private, encrypted tunnel across a public network such as the internet. Site-to-site VPNs connect whole offices; remote-access VPNs connect individual users to the corporate network.

deep.heading: Why VPNs
deep.text: The internet is cheap and everywhere but untrusted. A VPN protects data so that branch offices and home workers can use the internet as if it were a private link.

deep.heading: IPsec services
deep.text: IPsec provides confidentiality (encryption, e.g., AES), integrity (hashing, e.g., SHA), authentication (pre-shared keys or certificates), and anti-replay. ESP (IP protocol 50) provides encryption plus integrity; AH (IP protocol 51) provides integrity/authentication only and is rarely used. IKE negotiates keys on UDP 500; NAT traversal uses UDP 4500. Tunnel mode encrypts the entire original packet and adds a new IP header (typical for site-to-site).

deep.heading: Site-to-site vs remote access
deep.text: Site-to-site: VPN gateways (routers/firewalls) at each site build a permanent tunnel; hosts are unaware of it. GRE over IPsec adds support for multicast/routing protocols. Remote access: a client (e.g., Cisco Secure Client, formerly AnyConnect) on the user's device builds a tunnel on demand using TLS/SSL or IPsec; clientless SSL VPN uses only a web browser for limited access. v1.1 objective 5.5 asks you to describe IPsec remote access and site-to-site VPNs; configuration is not required.

lessons.why: Hybrid work and branch connectivity depend on VPNs. Understanding them helps you troubleshoot tunnels and choose the right design.

examples.title: Branch to HQ
examples.text: Two firewalls build an IPsec site-to-site tunnel over the internet, replacing an expensive leased line.

examples.title: Remote worker
examples.text: An employee launches the VPN client, authenticates with MFA, and receives an internal IP address.

mistakes: Thinking hosts must run VPN software for site-to-site VPNs.
Believing GRE alone encrypts traffic (it does not).
Confusing ESP (encrypts) with AH (no encryption).

terms.definition: Framework for securing IP traffic.
Encapsulating Security Payload (encrypts) / Authentication Header (no encryption).
Internet Key Exchange; negotiates security associations.
Per-user tunnel from a client to the corporate network.

memorize: IPsec: confidentiality, integrity, authentication, anti-replay.
ESP = protocol 50; AH = protocol 51; IKE = UDP 500; NAT-T = UDP 4500.
Site-to-site = gateway-to-gateway, always on; remote access = client-based, on demand.
examNotes: Expect comparison questions between site-to-site and remote-access VPNs.
lessons.summary: VPNs secure traffic across untrusted networks. IPsec provides confidentiality, integrity, authentication, and anti-replay for site-to-site tunnels; remote-access VPNs use client software with TLS or IPsec.

quiz.question: Which IPsec protocol provides encryption?
quiz.explanation: ESP encrypts; AH does not.

quiz.question: In a site-to-site VPN, which devices build the tunnel?
options: VPN gateways such as routers or firewalls
quiz.explanation: Gateways build site-to-site tunnels.

quiz.question: Which port does IKE use?
quiz.explanation: IKE uses UDP 500 (4500 with NAT-T).

blocks.title: Start with the problem
blocks.text: Two offices need private communication across a network they do not control. A VPN creates a protected logical relationship over that transport, but the outer path must still work and the endpoints must agree on identity and policy.

blocks.title: Build the mental model
blocks.text: IPsec uses negotiated security associations and policy to protect selected traffic. IKE negotiates identity/security parameters; ESP commonly supplies protected payload transport. Tunnel mode adds an outer IP header around the protected inner packet. Routing, traffic selection, NAT traversal, and MTU can all affect operation.

The local switch port

lessons.title: Wireless Security Protocols
lessons.simple: Wireless traffic can be captured by anyone nearby, so strong authentication and encryption are essential. Modern networks use WPA2 or WPA3, either with a shared passphrase (Personal) or with individual credentials via 802.1X (Enterprise).

deep.heading: Generations
deep.text: WEP: broken RC4-based encryption; never use. WPA: interim fix using TKIP. WPA2: AES-CCMP encryption; the long-time standard. WPA3: replaces PSK with SAE in Personal mode, requires Protected Management Frames (PMF), and offers a 192-bit security mode for Enterprise.

deep.heading: Personal vs Enterprise
deep.text: Personal (PSK/SAE) uses one passphrase for everyone — simple, suitable for homes and small offices. Enterprise uses 802.1X: the client (supplicant) authenticates through the AP/WLC (authenticator) to a RADIUS server (authentication server) using an EAP method (e.g., PEAP, EAP-TLS, EAP-FAST). Each user has unique credentials and keys.

deep.heading: Why SAE matters
deep.text: With WPA2-PSK, an attacker who captures the 4-way handshake can attempt an offline dictionary attack on the passphrase. WPA3's SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) resists offline dictionary attacks and provides forward secrecy. Open networks can use OWE (Enhanced Open) for encryption without a password. Configuring WPA2-PSK in the WLC GUI is covered in the WLAN GUI lesson.

lessons.why: Weak Wi-Fi security exposes the entire internal network to anyone in the parking lot.

examples.title: Corporate
examples.text: WPA2/WPA3-Enterprise with EAP-TLS certificates authenticates employees via Cisco ISE (RADIUS).

examples.title: Guest
examples.text: A separate guest SSID uses WPA3-Personal or OWE and a captive portal, mapped to an internet-only VLAN.

mistakes: Choosing TKIP for WPA2 (use AES).
Sharing one PSK with hundreds of employees in an enterprise.
Assuming WPA3 Personal still uses the same PSK handshake as WPA2.

terms.definition: Pre-Shared Key: common passphrase (WPA/WPA2 Personal).
Simultaneous Authentication of Equals (WPA3 Personal).
Port-based network access control using EAP and RADIUS.
Protected Management Frames.

memorize: WEP (RC4, broken) → WPA (TKIP) → WPA2 (AES-CCMP) → WPA3 (SAE, PMF, GCMP-256 in 192-bit mode).
Enterprise = 802.1X + EAP + RADIUS; Personal = PSK/SAE.
802.1X roles: supplicant, authenticator, authentication server.
examNotes: Know which protocol uses which encryption and authentication method.
lessons.summary: Use WPA2 (AES) or WPA3 (SAE, PMF). Personal mode uses a passphrase; Enterprise mode uses 802.1X/EAP with a RADIUS server for per-user authentication.

quiz.question: Which encryption does WPA2 use?
quiz.explanation: WPA2 uses AES-CCMP.

quiz.question: What does WPA3-Personal use instead of PSK?
quiz.explanation: Simultaneous Authentication of Equals.

quiz.question: In 802.1X, which role does the WLC/AP play?
quiz.explanation: The AP/WLC is the authenticator.

blocks.title: Start with the problem
blocks.text: A WLAN name is visible to everyone nearby. Security must establish who may join and protect the radio conversation; hiding the SSID is not a substitute for authentication and encryption.

blocks.title: Build the mental model
blocks.text: In an 802.1X design, the client is the supplicant, the AP/controller acts as authenticator, and an authentication server evaluates identity through the configured EAP method. Server-certificate validation matters for methods that use it. A successful association is not necessarily successful authentication or IP connectivity. Protected Management Frames requirements and transition modes depend on the security mode and platform.

lessons.title: Automation and Controller-Based Networking
lessons.simple: Traditionally, engineers configure each device by hand through the CLI. Automation and controllers let you define what you want once and push it to many devices consistently. Software-Defined Networking (SDN) moves decision-making to a central controller.

deep.heading: Why automate
deep.text: Manual configuration is slow, error-prone, and inconsistent. Automation reduces human error, speeds up changes, enforces standard configurations, and frees engineers for design work.

deep.heading: Planes and controllers
deep.text: Data plane: forwarding packets/frames (switching, routing lookups, ACL filtering, NAT). Control plane: building the information used for forwarding (routing protocols, STP, ARP). Management plane: device management (SSH, SNMP, syslog). In traditional networking, each device runs its own control plane and is managed individually. In controller-based networking, a controller centralizes the control/management logic and programs devices. The controller exposes a northbound interface (NBI), usually REST APIs, to applications and scripts, and uses southbound interfaces (SBIs) such as NETCONF, RESTCONF, OpenFlow, OpFlex, SSH/CLI, or SNMP to talk to devices.

deep.heading: SDN architectures: underlay, overlay, fabric
deep.text: Underlay: the physical network and its routing that provides IP reachability between devices. Overlay: virtual tunnels built on top of the underlay (e.g., VXLAN) that carry user traffic and create logical networks. Fabric: the combination of underlay and overlay managed as one system. In Cisco SD-Access, the underlay uses IS-IS, the overlay data plane uses VXLAN, the control plane uses LISP, and policy uses Cisco TrustSec (SGTs), all managed by Catalyst Center (formerly DNA Center). Traditional management: box-by-box, CLI, per-device changes. Controller-based (Catalyst Center): centralized intent-based policy, automation, assurance/analytics, and APIs.

lessons.why: Modern enterprise, data center, and WAN networks are increasingly controller-driven. Understanding planes and APIs is required to work with them.

examples.title: Adding a VLAN to 200 switches
examples.text: Traditional: log in to 200 switches. Controller-based: define the VLAN once in Catalyst Center or run one automation job that pushes it via APIs.

examples.title: SD-WAN
examples.text: A controller distributes routing and policy to branch routers; branches build encrypted overlay tunnels across any transport.

mistakes: Confusing northbound (to apps) and southbound (to devices) APIs.
Thinking SDN removes the data plane from devices; devices still forward traffic.
Mixing up underlay (physical) and overlay (virtual).

terms.definition: Forwarding of user traffic.
Protocols and processes that build forwarding tables.
Protocols used to manage devices.
Northbound (controller-to-app) / Southbound (controller-to-device) interfaces.
Virtual tunnel network / physical transport network.

memorize: Data plane forwards; control plane decides; management plane manages.
NBI = REST APIs to applications; SBI = NETCONF, RESTCONF, OpenFlow, OpFlex, CLI, SNMP.
SD-Access: IS-IS underlay, VXLAN data plane, LISP control plane.
Catalyst Center = former DNA Center.
examNotes: Expect to categorize functions into data/control/management planes.
lessons.summary: Automation and controllers replace box-by-box management with centralized, API-driven control. Know the three planes, NBI vs SBI, and underlay/overlay/fabric concepts.

quiz.question: Which plane does OSPF belong to?
quiz.explanation: Routing protocols are control plane.

quiz.question: A Python script calls the controller's REST API. Which interface is used?
quiz.explanation: Applications use the northbound API.

quiz.question: In SD-Access, which protocol provides the overlay data plane?
quiz.explanation: VXLAN encapsulates overlay traffic; LISP is the control plane.

blocks.title: Start with the problem
blocks.text: A team must apply one consistent policy to many switches. Repeating manual commands makes omissions easy. Automation expresses repeatable work; controller-based networking adds a coordinated view and interfaces for intent and device programming.

blocks.title: Build the mental model
blocks.text: Northbound APIs expose controller capabilities to applications; southbound interfaces connect controller functions to infrastructure. Underlay supplies transport reachability. Overlay supplies logical connectivity over that transport. A fabric combines coordinated components and policy. A controller does not eliminate the need for healthy underlay links, addressing, and routing.

blocks.title: Revisit the core explanation
blocks.text: Open this explanation when you are ready for the full mechanism.
items: Traditionally, engineers configure each device by hand through the CLI. Automation and controllers let you define what you want once and push it to many devices consistently. Software-Defined Networking (SDN) moves decision-making to a central controller.

blocks.title: Why this matters in practice
blocks.text: Open this explanation when you are ready for the full mechanism.
items: Modern enterprise, data center, and WAN networks are increasingly controller-driven. Understanding planes and APIs is required to work with them.

blocks.title: Why automate
blocks.text: Open this explanation when you are ready for the full mechanism.
items: Manual configuration is slow, error-prone, and inconsistent. Automation reduces human error, speeds up changes, enforces standard configurations, and frees engineers for design work.

blocks.title: Planes and controllers
blocks.text: Open this explanation when you are ready for the full mechanism.
items: Data plane: forwarding packets/frames (switching, routing lookups, ACL filtering, NAT). Control plane: building the information used for forwarding (routing protocols, STP, ARP). Management plane: device management (SSH, SNMP, syslog). In traditional networking, each device runs its own control plane and is managed individually. In controller-based networking, a controller centralizes the control/management logic and programs devices. The controller exposes a northbound interface (NBI), usually REST APIs, to applications and scripts, and uses southbound interfaces (SBIs) such as NETCONF, RESTCONF, OpenFlow, OpFlex, SSH/CLI, or SNMP to talk to devices.

blocks.title: SDN architectures: underlay, overlay, fabric
blocks.text: Open this explanation when you are ready for the full mechanism.
items: Underlay: the physical network and its routing that provides IP reachability between devices. Overlay: virtual tunnels built on top of the underlay (e.g., VXLAN) that carry user traffic and create logical networks. Fabric: the combination of underlay and overlay managed as one system. In Cisco SD-Access, the underlay uses IS-IS, the overlay data plane uses VXLAN, the control plane uses LISP, and policy uses Cisco TrustSec (SGTs), all managed by Catalyst Center (formerly DNA Center). Traditional management: box-by-box, CLI, per-device changes. Controller-based (Catalyst Center): centralized intent-based policy, automation, assurance/analytics, and APIs.

blocks.title: Separate the similar ideas
blocks.text: Traditional distributed control lets devices make protocol decisions locally. Controller-based designs centralize selected control/management functions while devices still forward traffic. The data plane moves packets, the control plane determines forwarding behavior, and the management plane configures/observes the system. Centralized logically does not mean one unprotected physical server.

blocks.text: In the SDN diagram, put applications above the controller and infrastructure below. Label northbound and southbound from the controller's perspective. Draw user traffic through the forwarding devices rather than automatically through the controller process.

blocks.title: Follow the behavior
blocks.text:
1. An operator submits intended policy.
2. The controller validates/translates it.
3. Infrastructure receives supported configuration or forwarding instructions.
4. Devices forward user packets.
5. Telemetry reports actual state.
6. The system compares intent with evidence. An API success response may mean acceptance, not completed convergence.

blocks.title: Adding a VLAN to 200 switches
blocks.text: Open this explanation when you are ready for the full mechanism.
items: Traditional: log in to 200 switches. Controller-based: define the VLAN once in Catalyst Center or run one automation job that pushes it via APIs.

blocks.title: SD-WAN
blocks.text: Open this explanation when you are ready for the full mechanism.
items: A controller distributes routing and policy to branch routers; branches build encrypted overlay tunnels across any transport.

learningStages.title: Configure
learningStages.reason: Objectives 6.1-6.3 explain architecture and impact. Controller APIs and device programming differ by product; this lesson does not invent a universal controller command.

blocks.title: What evidence should show
blocks.text: Inspect controller inventory, device reachability, task status, actual device configuration, and end-to-end service. Compare desired versus observed state. Verify high availability and failure behavior for the particular architecture; do not assume controller loss either stops all traffic or has no effect.

blocks.title: Diagnose, correct, and retest
blocks.text: If an overlay endpoint is unreachable, test underlay reachability before changing overlay policy. If a task is accepted but not realized, inspect per-device errors and permissions. Correct the failing dependency and verify actual forwarding, not just a green request status.

blocks.text: Use these checks when the evidence does not fit your first hypothesis.
items: Confusing northbound (to apps) and southbound (to devices) APIs.
Thinking SDN removes the data plane from devices; devices still forward traffic.
Mixing up underlay (physical) and overlay (virtual).

lessons.title: AI and Machine Learning in Network Operations
lessons.simple: Artificial intelligence and machine learning help operations teams spot problems sooner and work faster. Predictive AI learns what 'normal' looks like and flags anomalies or forecasts issues; generative AI creates content such as summaries, explanations, or configuration drafts from natural-language requests.

deep.heading: Basic definitions
deep.text: AI is the broad field of making machines perform tasks that normally need human intelligence. Machine learning (ML) is a subset of AI where systems learn patterns from data instead of being explicitly programmed. Supervised learning uses labeled data, unsupervised finds patterns in unlabeled data, and reinforcement learning learns through rewards.

deep.heading: Predictive AI in networking
deep.text: Learns baselines from telemetry (latency, client onboarding times, interface errors) and detects anomalies, predicts capacity exhaustion or failures, and correlates events to suggest root causes. Example: network assurance platforms flag that DHCP onboarding time at one site deviates from its learned baseline.

deep.heading: Generative AI and responsible use
deep.text: Generative AI (large language models) can answer natural-language questions about network state, summarize logs and incidents, draft configurations or documentation, and guide troubleshooting. Its output can be wrong (hallucinations), so engineers must validate generated configurations before deployment, protect sensitive data sent to AI services, and keep humans in control of changes.

lessons.why: AI-assisted operations reduce mean time to detect and resolve problems in large networks, and the v1.1 blueprint added this topic explicitly.

examples.title: Generative
examples.text: An engineer asks an AI assistant to summarize 2,000 syslog lines into the three most likely root causes, then verifies them manually.

lessons.title: REST APIs and JSON
lessons.simple: APIs let software talk to software. REST APIs use standard HTTP methods to create, read, update, and delete data, usually exchanging JSON. Controllers and modern network devices expose REST APIs so scripts can manage them.

deep.heading: REST and CRUD
deep.text: REST APIs use URIs to identify resources and HTTP verbs as actions: POST = Create, GET = Read, PUT = Update/replace, PATCH = partial update, DELETE = Delete. Responses carry status codes: 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content, 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized (not authenticated), 403 Forbidden (not permitted), 404 Not Found, 500 Internal Server Error.

deep.heading: REST characteristics and authentication
deep.text: Client-server, stateless (each request carries everything needed), cacheable, uniform interface, layered system (and optional code-on-demand). Authentication types: HTTP Basic (username/password, Base64-encoded, use only over HTTPS), API keys, bearer tokens (e.g., obtain a token then send it in an Authorization header), and OAuth. Data encoding: JSON, XML, or YAML, indicated by headers such as Content-Type: application/json.

deep.heading: JSON components
deep.text: Objects are enclosed in { } and contain key:value pairs separated by commas. Keys are strings in double quotes. Values can be a string ("Gi0/1"), number (1500), boolean (true/false), null, an object, or an array. Arrays are ordered lists in [ ]. Example: {"interface": {"name": "GigabitEthernet0/1", "enabled": true, "mtu": 1500, "ipv4": ["10.1.1.1/24"]}}. JSON has no comments, trailing commas are invalid, and whitespace is insignificant.

lessons.why: APIs and JSON are the language of automation. Even if you never write code, you must read API output and understand what a call does.

mistakes: Using single quotes in JSON (invalid; JSON requires double quotes).
Mapping PUT to Create (POST creates; PUT replaces/updates).
Confusing 401 (not authenticated) and 403 (authenticated but not allowed).

blocks.title: Start with the problem
blocks.text: A controller exposes device inventory through an API. Instead of scraping a screen, a client requests a resource and receives structured data. Understanding method, identity, status, and encoding prevents automation from treating every response as success.

blocks.title: Build the mental model
blocks.text: HTTP requests carry method, target, headers, and sometimes a body. HTTPS protects transport when certificate validation is correct. Authentication may use Basic over TLS, tokens, or other documented mechanisms; Base64 alone is not encryption. Idempotent methods describe intended effect of repetition, not identical responses or permission to retry every request blindly.

lessons.title: Configuration Management: Ansible and Terraform
lessons.simple: Configuration management tools apply consistent configuration to many devices automatically. Ansible pushes changes over SSH or APIs using YAML playbooks without installing agents. Terraform describes infrastructure as code and builds it to match the declared state.

deep.heading: Infrastructure as Code
deep.text: Instead of typing commands, you describe the desired configuration in text files stored in version control. The tool makes devices match the files, giving repeatable, reviewable, and reversible changes.

deep.heading: Ansible
deep.text: Red Hat Ansible is agentless and push-based. A control node connects to managed devices over SSH (or NETCONF/REST APIs). Key files: inventory (list of devices/groups), playbooks (YAML files with plays and tasks), modules (units of work such as cisco.ios.ios_config), and variables/templates (Jinja2). Ansible is written in Python and is widely used for network configuration.

deep.heading: Terraform and comparison
deep.text: HashiCorp Terraform is declarative infrastructure as code using HCL (HashiCorp Configuration Language). Providers interact with platforms (clouds, controllers, some network devices via APIs). Workflow: write → 'terraform plan' (preview changes) → 'terraform apply'. It tracks what it manages in a state file. Typical use: provisioning infrastructure (cloud networks, VMs, controller objects); Ansible typically configures devices and software. Older tools Puppet and Chef are agent-based and pull-based (supplementary; removed from v1.1).

lessons.why: Configuration management is how large networks stay consistent and how changes are reviewed and rolled back.

examples.title: Ansible playbook
examples.text: A playbook targets the 'access_switches' inventory group and ensures NTP servers and a login banner are configured on all of them.

examples.title: Terraform
examples.text: A Terraform file declares a cloud VPC, subnets, and security groups; 'terraform apply' creates them and records them in state.

mistakes: Thinking Ansible needs an agent on network devices.
Confusing YAML (Ansible) with HCL (Terraform).
Running 'terraform apply' without reviewing 'terraform plan'.

Terraform: declarative IaC, HCL, providers, plan/apply, state file.
Puppet/Chef (older): agent-based, pull model.

supplementary: Ansible can also use HTTP APIs and NETCONF modules, and Terraform can manage some network controllers; the exam focuses on the core characteristics listed above.

blocks.title: Start with the problem
blocks.text: A team needs consistent NTP and interface policy across many devices. Configuration management records desired work in reviewable files, but a repeatable mistake can spread faster than a manual one. Scope and validation matter as much as automation.

blocks.title: Build the mental model
blocks.text: Idempotence means repeated execution converges on the intended state without unnecessary change; it depends on the module/task/provider and design, not just the tool name. Terraform state can contain sensitive data and needs protected storage/locking. A plan previews proposed changes but does not prove they are operationally safe. Automation rollback requires captured prior state and a tested restoration path.

items: HashiCorp Terraform is declarative infrastructure as code using HCL (HashiCorp Configuration Language). Providers interact with platforms (clouds, controllers, some network devices via APIs). Workflow: write → 'terraform plan' (preview changes) → 'terraform apply'. It tracks what it manages in a state file. Typical use: provisioning infrastructure (cloud networks, VMs, controller objects); Ansible typically configures devices and software. Older tools Puppet and Chef are agent-based and pull-based (supplementary; removed from v1.1).

blocks.title: Separate the similar ideas
blocks.text: Ansible commonly runs agentless tasks from a control node over SSH or APIs using inventory, playbooks, modules, and variables. Terraform uses declarative configuration and providers to manage resources while tracking managed objects in state. They overlap in capability; Ansible is not limited to CLI and Terraform is not limited to public cloud.

blocks.title: Inspect the mechanism
blocks.text: Read the explanation for alternatives and assumptions; arrows are reading guides where stated.

blocks.title: Read the relationships
blocks.text: Follow two workflows: Ansible inventory -> playbook/tasks -> modules -> devices; Terraform configuration -> plan -> reviewed apply -> managed resources/state. Draw verification after both. Do not depict a plan as already changing the infrastructure.

blocks.title: Follow the behavior
blocks.text:
1. Select a small lab inventory.
2. Review variables and intended diff.
3. Run supported dry-run/check or plan behavior, understanding its limits.
4. Approve and apply only the intended scope.
5. Verify actual device/service state.
6. Repeat and inspect whether unnecessary changes recur. Store secrets outside ordinary lesson files.

blocks.title: Ansible playbook
blocks.text: Open this explanation when you are ready for the full mechanism.
items: A playbook targets the 'access_switches' inventory group and ensures NTP servers and a login banner are configured on all of them.

blocks.title: Terraform
blocks.text: Open this explanation when you are ready for the full mechanism.
items: A Terraform file declares a cloud VPC, subnets, and security groups; 'terraform apply' creates them and records them in state.

learningStages.title: Configure
learningStages.reason: Objective 6.6 recognizes capabilities. No runnable playbook/provider example is supplied without a defined lab inventory and supported module versions; the lesson teaches safe workflow and interpretation.

blocks.title: What evidence should show
blocks.text: Inspect targeted hosts/resources, task/plan output, actual configuration, and service tests. For Ansible, check mode support varies by module. For Terraform, review create/update/destroy actions and state handling. A successful tool exit is not a substitute for end-to-end verification.

blocks.title: Diagnose, correct, and retest
blocks.text: If a run targets too many devices, stop before applying and correct inventory/workspace/variables. If every repeat reports changes, inspect non-idempotent tasks, generated values, and drift. Do not delete Terraform state as a generic repair; it can orphan management relationships. Restore through a reviewed plan.

blocks.title: Mistakes to avoid
blocks.text: Use these checks when the evidence does not fit your first hypothesis.
items: Thinking Ansible needs an agent on network devices.
Confusing YAML (Ansible) with HCL (Terraform).
Running 'terraform apply' without reviewing 'terraform plan'.

blocks.title: Apply the idea
blocks.text: Which statement about idempotence is accurate?
items: It depends on the actual tasks/modules/providers and desired state
Every script is automatically idempotent
It means no configuration may ever change
It guarantees a safe production change
rationales: Tooling and task design determine repeat behavior.
A script can repeat destructive or unnecessary actions.
Convergence can require an initial change.
Repeatability does not prove correctness, scope, or operational safety.

blocks.title: Explain it in your own words
blocks.text: Ansible pushes configuration agentlessly using YAML playbooks over SSH/APIs; Terraform declaratively provisions infrastructure using HCL, providers, and a state file.

blocks.title: Facts worth retrieving from memory
blocks.text: Use these as retrieval prompts, not a replacement for the mechanism.
items: Ansible: agentless, push, SSH/API, YAML playbooks, Python.
Terraform: declarative IaC, HCL, providers, plan/apply, state file.
Puppet/Chef (older): agent-based, pull model.
